utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Popovic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody. All the accused are here. Representation is as yesterday, except that -- no, no, he's here. Okay. Representation is a full house today. Mr. Haynes is present. So, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecutor acknowledges that President Karadzic gave the order of the Krivaja operation directly to the Drina Corps, yet the Prosecutor alleges that the Main Staff was informed of the order of the Drina Corps on the 2nd of July, 1995. On the basis of these two presumptions, the Prosecution infers that General Miletic had knowledge of the order of President Karadzic and he received the order of the Drina Corps. First of all, those are only presumptions. Colonel Lasic was not certain how the Main Staff was informed of the order of President Karadzic. In fact, he was not certain whether the Main Staff had been informed. In the collection of the Drina Corps, no telegram informing the Main Staff of the order of General Karadzic was found. Also, there is no trace of any transmission of the order of the 2nd July 1995. Incidentally, General Miletic was -- is not the Main Staff. Even if one supposes that this information was transmitted to the Main Staff, this does not mean that they were automatically transmitted to General Miletic. The order of President Karadzic may have been given directly or reported directly to General Mladic. It could have also been transmitted by a go-between of the duty officer. The onus of proof lies with the Prosecutor. The knowledge of the information concerning military activities around Srebrenica, and in particular the order of the 2nd July 1995, is an important fact. The Prosecutor should have established, beyond any reasonable doubt, that General Miletic had received this information, yet he did not do so. No evidence in the case file permits to reach such a conclusion. Indeed, if such information were destined to General Miletic, it should have been found in the reports to the Main Staff. These reports do mention the preparation of combat activities but similar information can also be found in a large number of previous reports from the Drina Corps as well as from the Main Staff, and in particular the report of the 16th of May, 1995, P2892 and P2896. The reports of 2, 3, and 4 July were not drafted on the basis of the order for the combat activities or on the basis of an order of President Karadzic. They were drafted on the basis of the order received from -- on the basis of the reports received from the Drina Corps. Let's take as an example the report of the Main Staff of the 4th of July, 1995, P3164. The sentence quoted by the Prosecutor at the footnote 4150, concerning the closing up of the enclaves, is taken -- lifted from the report of the 4 July 1995, 5D1106. The closing of the enclaves was not a new task for the Drina Corps. It was its permanent task, which appears from all the work plans of the commander of the Drina Corps, as shown by 5D989 to 5D995. No particular knowledge of General Miletic of the actions in which the Drina Corps was going to be engaged on the 6th of July, 1995, appears from the reports drafted by General Miletic, who, on the 7th of July, 1995, was going to Belgrade to spend some time with his family. The Prosecutor has adduced no evidence that General Miletic has taken part in the making of decisions concerning the changes of the initial plan and of the entering in of the VRS in Srebrenica. Indeed, as I just said, at the time General Miletic was not even at the Main Staff. During the hearing of 2nd September 2008, the Prosecutor stated that he did not deny the alibi of General Miletic, and he considered for his case that the alibi was proven. The Defence has no obligation to prove the alibi. The Defence is simply obliged to present evidence giving rise to a reasonable doubt as for the evidence adduced by the Prosecutor. It behooves the Prosecutor to set aside the reasonable hypothesis which the alibi is true, or to prove the alleged facts, despite the alibi invoked by the Defence. The decision to enter Srebrenica was taken on the 9th of July, 1995; P33. No evidence exists that General Miletic would have had any knowledge of this decision before he heard that the Army of the Republika Srpska had, indeed, entered Srebrenica. Also, nothing in the case file shows that General Miletic could have known that such a decision was going to be made or that he could have foreseen it. Now, this is a decision which changed the course of the operation. General Miletic was completely unaware of it, just as he was unaware of the order of the 10th of July, 1995, P181. Simply, he was not present at the Main Staff. We consider that General Miletic was not the member of a joint criminal enterprise. In addition, as he had no prior knowledge of the decision of 9 July, he could in no way foresee that acts such as opportunistic killings might be committed. The Prosecutor had difficulty in explaining how General Miletic could have foreseen such matters and gave no explanation, more or less. The Appeals Chamber therefore decided, in its recent decision in the Karadzic case, that the possibility for a crime to be committed must be sufficiently substantiated to be foreseeable for the accused. Without knowing the -- that the Army of Republika Srpska was going to enter Srebrenica, General Miletic had no way of foreseeing that the population of Srebrenica was going to take refuge in Potocari. The conditions in Potocari, separating the men, and the detention at Bratunac, Kravica, and Petkovci was completely unforeseeable for him. Therefore, he could not foresee the possibility for the alleged acts in paragraph 31 of the indictment. The allegation of the Prosecutor according to which General Miletic was at the center of the decision-making process in the period which followed the taking of Srebrenica is always totally unfounded, and the evidence cited by the Prosecutor do not confirm this. I shall not repeat the arguments concerning the document of the 13th July 1995, P192, because we have already put them in our closing brief, paragraphs 508 to 513, but I would like to say a few words on the alleged participation of General Miletic in the drafting of the order of the 13th July 1995, P45. The Prosecutor cites the decision Nedeljko Trkulja -- the declaration of Nedeljko Trkulja was based exclusively on the fact that this order bears number 03/4 of the 11th of September, 2007, page 15183, yet Nedeljko Trkulja admitted in fact that he did not know who had written this order; page 15215. Document P45 bears number 03/4, just as practically any other order of the Main Staff. In 1995 and up to the 17th of July, 1995, General Miletic was the only officer in charge of operational matters in the Main Staff, since Ljubomir Obradovic was on sick leave. Simply stated, he could not have drafted alone all the orders given by General Mladic, General Milovanovic, and the assistants of the commander. The order of the 13th of July, 1995, bears the number 03/4-1629. This number, 1629, means that as from the 1st of January and until the 13th of July, 1995, the Main Staff had given 1.629 orders, 1.629 orders, by -- so an average of eight to nine orders were issued every day from the Main Staff, 03/4 of -- even if one assumes that General Miletic did nothing else, he was not able to draft alone every day eight to nine orders. The Prosecutor admits that officers of other bodies were involved in operational affairs. The duty officers who came from were different sectors certainly perfectly capable of drafting orders. When they were on duty, those officers, just like duty officers of subordinate units, the corps and the brigades, were not subordinate to the chief of the body in charge of operational matters, but to the commander or the person who stood in for the commander. This is 7D442. Besides, the Defence of General Gvero does not challenge that General Gvero gave orders bearing number 03/4. In their final brief, page 94, footnote 408, and page 209, paragraph 297, the Defence of General Gvero has acknowledged that General Gvero had given the order of the 11th July 1995. This is Exhibit 6D207. This order of the 11th of July, 1995, 6D207, bears, just as the order of the 13th of July, 1995, the number 03/4. In order to prove that General Miletic had taken part in the drafting of an order, the Prosecutor should have adduced the evidence showing that General Miletic had, indeed, done so. The evidence shows that General Miletic was not the only officer who drafted orders in the Main Staff, and no evidence shows that he would have taken part in the drafting of the order of the 13th of July, 1995. The Defence of General Miletic does not challenge that the logistic body of the Main Staff could have been involved in certain logistic aspects of the activities of the Drina Corps in July 1995, but General Miletic had no part in this. As we indicated, General Miletic is neither the Main Staff nor the commander of the Main Staff. He has no need to know all the activities of the Main Staff and may not, therefore, be held responsible for them. I would simply like to add that the allegations of the Prosecutor in paragraph 287 of their final closing brief, concerning the use of air bombs during Krivaja operation, are unfounded, the Prosecutor alleges also, at the the footnote 674, that General Miletic was involved in the transportation of such bombs, air bombs. Quoting document 5D976 and the testimony of Dragisa -- neither the testimony of Dragisa Masal, nor the document 5D976, have any connection with the Krivaja operation, and document 5D976, which is the order of General Milovanovic of the 30th March, 1995, and the testimony of Dragisa Masal concerned the Operation Spreca. Milo Gavric, chief of the artillery of the Bratunac Brigade stated that these bombs, although provided for in the Brigade order of 5 July 1995, were never used. Just as there is no evidence implicating General Miletic in logistic affairs, the Prosecutor did not adduce any evidence that would have involved General Miletic in the mobilisation of the buses. The case of the Defence concerning the conversation or intercept concerning fuel on 12th of July, 1995, P111, are expounded in our closing brief, paragraphs 418-483. This is P1111. In his interpretation of the intercept, the Prosecutor, supposing that Miletic was mentioned in this conversation was General Miletic, is only interested neither in what General Miletic did, nor in what he said, he is not even interested in what General Miletic knew. For him it is enough that somebody, whose identity is not known, would have contacted him. If the Miletic mentioned in this intercept is General Miletic, this conversation, contrarily-wise to allegations, shows exactly the opposite of what the Prosecutor wants to demonstrate. It shows that General Miletic has in no way contributed to the supply of fuel and that he did not even have knowledge of this, because in any other case he should have reacted to the request of fuel which he received, and he did not do so. Indeed, there is no evidence that General Miletic has had any role concerning the events which follow the fall of Srebrenica until the Muslim column created a military threat in the area of the Zvornik Brigade. Although we consider that the actions taken with the intention to military combat the column do not feature in the indictment, I would like to make a few remarks on the conclusions of the Prosecution which are unfounded. Could we please go to closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Supposing this conversation did take place. Is it really so important to know whether it took place on the 14th or the 15th of July? Well, of course it's important. All -- the whole case for the Prosecutor is predicated on this conversation, which would have given General Miletic, in the evening of the 14th July 1995, the information concerning the column and the situation in Zvornik. If General Miletic ever had such a conversation, he certainly didn't have it on the 14th of July, 1995. We have set out our arguments regarding conversations connected with extension 155. This was P1164. And with the conversation a certain General Vilotic may have had, P1166, in our closing brief, paragraphs 530 to 540. Nobody in this case has ever managed to identify General Vilotic. Regarding extension 155, this extension could be anything, anywhere. But if it is - if it is - the extension of the Main Staff, it first -- it had to be established at least who was in the operations room in the evening of 14th July of 1995. There were always many officers in that room. There were duty officers, for sure, and Witness Sasa Jovanovic did confirm that the assistant commanders could have been there. He said so on the 6th of July, 2009, transcript pages 33949. The possibility that General Miletic might have taken up the phone on extension 155 is only one among many other possibilities that are equally reasonable and plausible. Many other officers could have taken up the phone on extension 155. To conclude that it was General Miletic is certainly not the only reasonable conclusion. The way the conversation between Malinic and Nastic, which is P1168, on 14th of July, is also wrong. If the Prosecutor is to be believed, Zoran Malinic gave instructions to Nastic after speaking with General Miletic. The words put into Malinic's mouth by the Prosecutor were, indeed, spoken by Nastic, because he was the one who gave instructions to Malinic. Even if you think that this conversation was true, which has not been confirmed by other evidence, this does not support the Prosecutor's case. Nastic did not speak with General Miletic, and the instructions he gave, which were incorrectly attributed to Malinic by the Prosecutor, have no link whatsoever with General Miletic. If you analyse the events and the conversations of the 14th of July, 1995, correctly, you will see that on that day General Miletic did not have any information as to the situation prevailing in the Drina Corps area of responsibility, other than what he could read in reports. The report of the Main Staff of the 14th of July, 1995, P48, literally passes on the information provided by the Drina Corps in their report, which is 4D84. If General Miletic had other information, he would have put it into the Main Staff report, just as he did on the 16th of July, 1995, P50, when he had received information from other sources. General Miletic informed the Zvornik Brigade of the arrival of the Krajina Corps Brigade. This is not an order. It is a piece of information drafted after an agreement with the 1st Corps commander. But beyond these rather technical observations, is it possible to see, in this document, an unlawful act, an unusual act, or a piece of document that should not have been written? No. This document is a military document that was written with the sole -- with the unique objective of fighting the Muslim forces. And we're not just speaking about the column that left Srebrenica. We have in mind also the 2nd Corps forces that attacked the area of the Zvornik Brigade on the north-west front. This is 5D303. This was the testimony of Ostoja Stanisic on the 17th of May, 2007; transcript pages 11713. The dispatch of reinforcements to Zvornik on the 15th of July was a militarily-justified act. This is the only possible conclusion. No criminal intent can be inferred from this act. When General Miletic passed on the information regarding the dispatch of the Krajina Brigade to Zvornik, he had not the slightest idea of what was really happening in Zvornik. He couldn't even imagine that the members of that brigade could later on be involved in criminal acts of which, incidentally, General Miletic is not accused and that were totally, in all respects, inconceivable for him. The only acts that could have been ascribed to General Miletic on the 15th, 16th, and 17th of July, 1995, are all linked to the military threat that was represented by the forces of the ABiH, by the column, but also by the 2nd Corps forces. Regarding the allegations of the Prosecution that General Miletic had knowledge of murder, executions, this is way beyond the scope of the indictment. But beyond that, the Prosecutor's conclusions are implausible constructions, devoid of any evidence. The reports General Miletic received at the time were very vague. They were also contradictory, and none of them managed to describe the situation properly. General Miletic was not in the field, he was not in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. No information regarding the thousands of Muslims that had been captured and detained ever reached him. The only thing that was reported to him was the fact that a large number of Muslims had surrendered. In a fighting situation, a large number can amount to several scores of prisoners. Neither General Miletic nor the Administration for Operations and Training had any authority regarding prisoners. General Miletic could only include this information in the reports drafted by the Main Staff. This was his obligation, and this is what he did. He could not imagine for a single moment what was the fate -- what could be the fate of these prisoners. Once again, General Miletic is not the Main Staff. He did not receive all the reports sent to the Main Staff. He received combat reports. The reports on intelligence mentioned by the Prosecutor in paragraph 1702 of their brief were not addressed to General Miletic. Document P149 was not even sent to the Main Staff. Documents P147 and P148 were sent to the Administration for Intelligence, the Intelligence Sector. There is no evidence to confirm that General Miletic ever saw them. There is no evidence to show that General Miletic should have seen them. Just as he was not involved in the Srebrenica events, General Miletic did not take part in the Zepa events. General Mladic was in Zepa, and so were some of his assistant commanders. It is obvious that those who were in Zepa knew the situation in Zepa much better than General Miletic, who was not there. The only knowledge he had was derived from the reports he would receive. With regard to the report of the 65 Protection Regiment that was sent by telephone, it was about the activities of the said regiment on their base in Crna Rijeka, where the unit was in charge of securing the Main Staff. These reports did not contend any information about Zepa. The latter was to be found in the Drina Corps reports to which one unit of the 65 -- 65th Regiment had been re-subordinated by way of an order given by General Milovanovic on the 21st of May, 1995. This is Exhibit 5D1214. Admittedly, during the Zepa operation, General Miletic did receive some request from the field, but these documents do not amount to any evidence of his contribution to the Zepa events. Very simply -- to put it very simply, there is no evidence that the requests addressed to him were ever followed up. There is no evidence to suggest that General Tolimir received the communications equipment asked for on the 14th of July. This was P183. There is no evidence to show that the military police of the 65th Regiment requested by General Krstic on the 20th of July - this was P3015 - ever made it to Zepa. There is no evidence that the proposals made by General Tolimir and sent on the 21st of July - P2794 - were ever implemented. The Defence has set out their arguments about the conversation between General Mladic and General Krstic in their brief; paragraphs 568 to 572. Let me just say this: Exhibit P3058, which show, the Prosecutor alleges, confirms the content of the conversation, shows, indeed, contrary to the Prosecutor's allegation and contrary to the content of the conversation, throughout the day on 17th of July, 1995, the Muslims turned down the conditions offered by the Serbs. Indeed, General Mladic would not have the meeting at the airport, but the negotiations between the Serbs and the Muslims, mediated through the UNPROFOR, carried on after the refusal, and an answer was expected the next day at 10.00. Within the context of Exhibit P3058, the contents of the conversation that bears the number P1231 is totally unlogical [as interpreted]. On that day, the 17th of July, Colonel Trkulja returned from Zvornik. Zvornik may have been the reason why General Krstic had to contact Colonel Miletic. Zvornik, Zepa, and why not the Drina Corps unit that was on the Sarajevo front? Why not the reports that General Miletic had been expecting since December that are mentioned in conversation P2341? Zepa is certainly not the only possible topic of this conversation. There is no evidence to substantiate the conversation between General Mladic and General Krstic. There is no evidence that General Krstic ever contacted General Miletic. May I remind you of the testimony of Witness PW-147, who testified that at times the events that would follow a conversation were exactly the opposite of what had been said in that conversation. Indeed, after the Prosecutor corrected their allegation about Colonel Miljanovic, and after the conversation -- about the conversation of 24th of July, the only link between Miletic and Zepa remains Exhibit P190, a report about Colonel Karanovic on the 25th of July. Contrary to the Prosecutor's allegation, this exhibit does not show that General Miletic talked to General Lugonja. Regarding the conversation with Mr. Bulajic, this exhibit does not allow the inference that General Miletic spoke with him or whether he was just present during the conversation. The conversation with Mr. Bulajic is about negotiations carried out by the RS Commission for War Prisoners with Muslim authorities. Such negotiations are nothing uncommon. They should have been useful and constructive. Their purpose was not to transfer population; it was to look for a solution. General Miletic's participation in the conversation with Mr. Bulajic does not mean that he contributed to the JCE, let alone that he had any intent to do so. General Smith went to Zepa. He participated in the negotiations. He was far more involved than General Miletic was. However, it never occurred to anyone to say that General Smith would have participated in forcible transfer. The only difference between General Smith and General Miletic is that General Smith was a member of the UNPROFOR, whilst General Miletic was a VRS member. The fact of belonging to the VRS is not enough to infer General Miletic's criminal intent, but nothing, not a single shred of evidence, would prove that General Miletic, throughout his service in the VRS throughout the war, including in 1995, ever acted with a criminal intent. General Miletic was not in Srebrenica, he was not in Zepa. He lacked any specific information related to these events. And, above all, he had no influence at all. General Miletic knew that General Smith was going to Zepa. He knew that the international organisations were in Zepa. How could he assume that acts that can be characterised as criminal acts may have happened there? Of course, the mere presence of international organisations does not remove the criminal character from the act of transferring population. It is just that General Miletic was not there, that he had no accurate information regarding these events. He could not know that criminal acts could have been committed. In his view, the fact that there were international organisations there was a guarantee, an assurance, that the laws of war would be complied with. All the acts of General Miletic were perfectly legitimate, were carried out as part of his duties. Of course, a legitimate act that was accomplished as part of somebody's duties can also contribute to a criminal enterprise, but, at any rate, it must be established that the act had been carried out with criminal intent. Yet, the evidence adduced at trial does not allow any such inference. The acts that could be ascribed to General Miletic would have been carried out by any officer in the position of the chief of the Main Staff Operations and Training. Any officer in charge of operations would have done exactly the same as General Miletic, and no officer in charge of operations could have done -- would have done anything else. Mr. President, Your Honours, you don't have in front of you the entire Army of Republika Srpska. You do not have the Main Staff in front of you. You do not have to make any determination on the duties of the chief of the Administration for Operations and Training. You have to make findings as to General Miletic's responsibility. He was an officer who, as part of his duties, took part in drafting Directive 7, but he was also the officer who did not transmit the final text of that directive to subordinate units. General Miletic was in a position to sign notifications regarding convoys when General Milovanovic was absent. He had no influence whatsoever on the decisions that were made, but he knew that the convoy would not be allowed through if he did not send a notification. General Miletic was not the person who was -- whom it was impossible to bypass in the Main Staff. The entire Krivaja operation took place while he was on leave. General Miletic did not take part in making the decision. He had no influence over General Mladic. He wasn't even directly subordinated to him. He was subordinated to General Milovanovic. This trial went on for over three years. Several thousands of exhibits were admitted, but there is none whatsoever showing a meeting between General Mladic and General Miletic. There is no evidence or suggestion that a proposal made was ever made by General Miletic to General Mladic. There is no evidence of any specific contact between General Miletic and General Mladic. There is nothing, but for General Mladic's speech that failed to mention among -- as people being among his close associates General Miletic. He's a discreet and decent officer. He's an officer who never expressed, in a conversation, an interview, or a speech, the slightest animosity or bias towards ethnic communities. General Miletic was also a moderate officer. That General Mladic sent for the first time to a meeting with the UNPROFOR in September 1995, when the balance of power had shifted and when General Mladic had to display cooperation and moderation. Mr. President, Your Honours, the evidence adduced at trial fails to establish General Miletic's responsibility. The Prosecutor failed to establish, beyond reasonable doubt, that General Miletic had any criminal intent. Therefore, General Miletic must be acquitted of all charges. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Kwon? Judge Stole? Judge Prost? None of us has any questions for you at this stage, at least. We may have later on, after having heard everyone. So -- yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I had the opportunity last evening to review the transcript of yesterday's proceedings, and with your kind permission I would request the opportunity to supplement just three of the answers that I gave you yesterday very briefly, certainly less than six or seven minutes. And I understand that we actually came in under our time allotment by about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I'd like to begin with a question that was asked by Her Honour Judge Prost, who asked -- and I apologise that I don't have the official page references, but Judge Prost asked: "Let's presume that there is a conclusion reached that at least two members of Mr. Borovcanin's unit had custody, just for the sake of argument." And then a question followed about the legal implications of the Mrksic decision. I should at that point have presented to you, first of all, a factual issue, and that is that by the time Mr. Borovcanin arrives along the road, one of those two men is dead and the other has left, so I suggest to you that in respect at least of those two individuals, custody cannot be attributed to Mr. Borovcanin because one is dead, one is gone. That's the first argument. But this leads to a second question which I believe was interrelated to the question that Her Honour Judge Prost was asking, or at least it is in substance, and that was the President's question being, and I quote: "Why would there be those two specials and no one else from the specials?" And I have two submissions on this. First, I simply wish to draw your attention more specifically to our brief at 190 to 192, where I more fully set out the substantiation to the answer that I gave yesterday. But much more importantly, even if you're left in doubt about why those two individuals were there, and we respectfully submit that if you are in doubt, that doubt must be resolved in favour of the accused, but even if you were to decide otherwise, I suggest to you that there is a huge body of evidence that you need to consider, in addition to just the absence of a "why," in determining whether or not that is a safe inference. In fact, we devote a substantial portion of our brief precisely to addressing that wider context so that you can assess whether the remainder of that unit can be inferred to have been there just on the basis of the presence of those two individuals. And that evidence is summarised in the bullets presented at paragraph 369, and I simply refer you to that paragraph because it conveniently summarises the evidence that precedes that paragraph. The third question that I would like to address you on is Judge Stole's question, which I must say I didn't particularly -- I did not answer particularly well, having gone back and looked at the transcript. He asked a particular question in relation to a sentence that appears in the middle of paragraph 330 of our brief, and the sentence is: "Borovcanin had no duty, as a superior, to make any inquiries into what was going on in the warehouse unless his men were present there." Let me try to explain what I meant by that. Article 7(3) requires a commander to ensure that one's own subordinates are not committing crimes. It doesn't give rise to an open-ended obligation to inquire as to whether non-subordinates are giving crimes -- are committing crimes. Borovcanin did make inquiries as to whether his men were committing crimes, and I refer you to paragraphs 328 to 330 of our brief, where we do set out the inquiries that he did make at that time and subsequently. We argue there and we believe that it is reasonable for you to accept that it was reasonable for him to rely on what he was told at that time, given the context. And this is a fact-specific inquiry. Given the context, it was reasonable for him to rely on what he was told. And in that respect, again, the contextual factors that make it reasonable for him to have relied on what he was told are expressed at that paragraph 369, in the bullet points, but also as illustrated in Annex F of our brief, which shows you where his units were along the road. So the basis for the claim that is being made in the middle of paragraph 330, to answer this question very directly, is a factual -- that's a factual claim based upon what we know of the evidence. That's not intended to be a legal claim to suggest that there was no duty to make those inquiries. He did make those inquiries. And for completeness, I would also refer you, in addition to paragraphs 328 to 330, also to paragraphs 336 to 338, where further inquiries and explanations are documented. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Judge Prost? Judge Stole? Okay. Now, do you need some time to -- no, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, it's now our opportunity to address you on behalf of Milan Gvero. Your Honours, I'm going to start, then Mr. Krgovic is going to take over a little later on, and then I'm going to take up where he leaves off. Let me begin by saying that making closing speeches used to be my bread and butter. Prior to my arriving at this Tribunal, over a 20-year period I must have given literally hundreds of such addresses both for the prosecution and for the defence. These were in front of magistrates, judges, and juries, in trials that lasted from as little as one hour to as long as several months, trials in relation to a whole range of criminal allegations, from the very minor to the very serious. The problem, Your Honours, that I face today is that I'm somewhat out of practice. I've worked at this Tribunal for over four years, and I have never, in that time, given an address like this. I can only hope that in the next hour or so, I will learn that making a closing address is a little like riding a bicycle, something that one can always do once one has learned how, a truism, of course, confirmed to me by living in the Netherlands. The main reason I'm emphasising this at the beginning of my address is not to ask you to excuse my lack of organisational skill, which all around me know only too well, or even my lack of eloquence. It's that you forgive me if at times I sound like an old, broken record as I address the Court endlessly about the basic tenet of any fair system of criminal justice; namely, the burden and standard of proof. This is, in part, because old habits die hard, and such a theme would be the central part of any such address that I have given in the past, but it's also because it's a subject that I feel is worth spending some of our valuable time upon today. And in one sense, let me say I feel a little like Mr. Ostojic. He said he was somewhat apologetic for having mentioned the subject at all, because like him, I appreciate that this Trial Chamber is very familiar with this concept. I appreciate it will always be in the forefront of your minds, that you are professional judges, and that you neither need nor appreciate being lectured by counsel on this important subject. But the simple fact, we suggest, that with the best will in the world, it's all too easy to get it slightly wrong and mis-apply this vital principle. During the course of the addresses we've heard over the last few days, we've seen that, and simply by way of example and illustration I would like to, over the next few minutes, highlight to you how easy it is to get it wrong. And I'm about to give, if I may, a random selection relating to various accused in this case, and they're purely in chronological order. In fact, the first my learned friend Madame Fauveau just referred to a few moments ago, but I make no apologies for making the same point as she has just done. At 34072, on the 2nd of September, Mr. Thayer was addressing her case, and he said: "Obviously, from our position during trial and in our brief, we're not contesting in any real way General Miletic's quasi-alibi of being in Belgrade from the 7th through the 11th. Let's assume that it's been proved just for the sake of argument." Well, Your Honours, quite what Mr. Thayer meant by "we're not contesting in any real way," is, to put it mildly, somewhat obscure. But leaving that aside, he's got it wrong. He said, "Let's assume that it's been proven." Well, of course, Miletic doesn't have to prove anything at all, least of all an alibi. Two pages later, Mr. Thayer says: "You have to ignore a mountain of compelling testimony to come to the conclusion that DutchBat was sitting on that much fuel at that time." We say he's wrong. The Defence do not need to establish any such conclusion at all. The opposite is true. You'd have to be satisfied, beyond a reasonable doubt, that the only conclusion was that DutchBat were not sitting on that much fuel. At 34083, Mr. Thayer's addressing my client's case, and he says: "The Gvero brief would literally have you believe ..." This makes it sound, we suggest, like we have a burden, something we have to prove. Let's make it clear, Your Honours. We're not seeking to make you believe anything at all. The only purpose of our final brief in these submissions is to contend that the Prosecution have failed to discharge their heavy burden. If we suggest anything at all, it's literally in that context. The following day, at 34181, Mr. Elderkin is addressing a Gvero Defence factual point about a particular alleged opportunistic killing. He says: "It is not reasonable to draw any conclusion." Again, we suggest it's the wrong test. The Defence have no burden, nor are they seeking to persuade you to draw any conclusions at all. On the 4th of September, Mr. McCloskey is addressing Mr. Borovcanin's case, and he says: "It was full of unreasonable conclusions." Again, we'd suggest the wrong test, but he goes on a line later and he says this: "We absolutely stand by, as we always have, the legal proposition, if there are two reasonable interpretations of circumstantial evidence, one in favour of the Defence and one in favour of the Prosecution, the Court must go with the version in favour of the Defence." Now, Mr. McCloskey makes it sound like some sort of equal contest. Perhaps he doesn't mean quite what he says, but we would suggest it's misleading and, at the very best, a simplification of what is a vital topic. At 34239, Mr. McCloskey says: "The fair inference you should make is ..." Again, wrong test, we suggest, Your Honours. The only inferences or tests, from the Prosecution's point of view, if it's anything less than the only inference you can act on in the Prosecution's favour, then it's not an inference that you can draw adverse to an accused in this case. Even my learned friend Mr. Gosnell, in his tour de force on Wednesday, at 34573, got it wrong when he said: "The Defence side are required to discharge ..." Of course, the Defence are not required to discharge anything whatsoever. And, finally, I hope you'll forgive me, but Madame Fauveau, we suggest, got it wrong yesterday when, at 34648, she said: "It suffices," she's talking about the Defence here, "for it to adduce evidence showing that another possibility is reasonable." Well, of course the Defence don't have to adduce any evidence at all. Now, Your Honours may say that these are slips of the tongue, and in some cases no doubt they are. Some may be stylistic and some may be translation, interpretation, or that type of error. But we suggest that they do indicate how easy it is to enter into a general misconception as to exactly what the burden of standard of proof is and what the words "beyond reasonable doubt" mean. And when the Prosecution advocates were saying these particular things, perhaps they weren't considering quite what these words mean and the extent to which they apply to this and any other case. Now, before I move on, simply because it fits conveniently into this part of my address, I'd like to deal with another similar point that arises in the Prosecution final brief, and it's been alluded to in one form or another, I think, by both Mr. Bourgon and Madame Fauveau in slightly different contexts. But so far as Gvero is concerned, 1765 of that brief, the Prosecution say: "Gvero would have participated in the drafting of Directive 7." We suggest, Your Honours, that the words by the drafter of that sentence "would have" give the game away. The writers of the Prosecution final brief are native English speakers, and they could easily have said Gvero participated in the drafting of Directive 7. Because they know they don't have the evidence to support that proposition, subconsciously or otherwise, we suggest, they put in the words "would have." And in this context, the words "would have" fall short of beyond reasonable doubt. We make a similar point in relation to paragraph 1760. Returning to where I left off a moment ago, it's a basic principle that the accused doesn't have to prove anything at all. The presumption of innocence means precisely what it says. It does not mean, and excuse me for putting it this way, that the Prosecution are entitled to say, somewhat emotively, "These are terrible crimes, there are lots of victims that require justice, the accused in question has a close connection with the army who committed these crimes, look who this accused associates with, this is all terribly, terribly suspicious, dodgy, fishy, call it what you will. The accused must be guilty, or put another way, unless the accused comes up with some compelling description that sounds correct, that he must be guilty." Your Honours, we suggest it's all too easy to slip into that kind of thinking, particularly in a case that centers on an allegation of quite literally the murder of thousands of people. Now, if you'd excuse me, but I want to broaden this out very slightly and look at this particular topic in a slightly different way, and in the context of a trial by judge rather than jury, because, as you're no doubt aware, juries are viewed as sacrosanct in many countries, but even their staunchest defenders would have to admit they have one very significant drawback, and that is they give no reasons at all for their decisions. And it's here that the parties to this case, both Prosecution and Defence, have a distinct advantage, we suggest. The parties will learn the reasons why a Trial Chamber has come to its various conclusions. This, of course, provides a very important safe-guard. The judgement and its various conclusions will allow the parties to know how the Trial Chamber has evaluated the various witnesses it has heard, as well as the other evidence, but, of course, such evaluations and, in particular, conclusions, need to be within the context of the burden the standard of proof. The parties will be able to see why a particular witness, in whole or in part, has been relied upon by the Trial Chamber. It's a basic tenet of the system that this is a very unequal battle. I say "a very unequal battle" because it's heavily weighed in favour of an accused person, because - and excuse me for stating the obvious - for you to rely on a witness or a piece of evidence in the Prosecution's favour, you would need to be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that that piece of evidence or witness was correct in that regard. Of course, to rely upon a witness or a piece of evidence in an accused's favour, there only needs to be some reasonable possibility that what the Defence assert about that piece of evidence is, in fact, correct. We suggest that one needs to be realistic about this, because it follows that in this or, indeed, any other trial, there are highly likely to be very much issues that the Trial Chamber, in its judgements, are actually unable to determine. What do I mean by this? Well, on any given issue, if the Trial Chamber are left in any reasonable doubt about the issue, then, of course, they have to give the benefit of that doubt to an accused. Now, addressing this full on and being, for wont of a better expression, adult about it, this does not mean for one moment that the Prosecution case on any hypothetical issue is wrong; indeed, it may well be right. On many occasions, it probably is right. Equally, it doesn't mean that a Defence case on a particular issue is right or probably right; indeed, it's wrong or quite probably wrong. But if there's a reasonable doubt, that always exercises in favour of the accused. We venture to suggest that this leaves a Trial Chamber in a long, complicated case like this, in some difficulty. Real istically, the desire and certainly the temptation in a judgement is to try and make a series of factual findings so as to, in effect, tell an account, dare say a historical account, of these events, and then fit the accused into the picture. But we would venture to suggest that it's not like writing a report on these events in the way that NIOD were able to or, indeed, the way that the Secretary-General was able to. It's not like writing a historical account in the way that various books one could buy in a shop read. It's actually, we would venture to suggest, much more difficult as it's far more disjunctive. Now, Your Honours, I appreciate that when I am saying this, I am addressing Judges who have had the experience of writing judgements at this Tribunal hitherto, but nonetheless I persist with my point. The problem, we suggest, that the nature of the system at the ICTY is, in fact, totally inimical to this type of fact-finding, and it's inimical to that because in order to say that any fact, and we quite literally mean any fact as established, you've got to be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that the Prosecution have proved it. And to repeat what I've said, this is actually highly unlikely on many contentious issues. Common sense simply dictates that you are going to be left in doubt, that you're going to say, Well, we think that this probably happened, or, Yes, this has been proved on the balance of probabilities, but we have to accept that a reasonable doubt has been raised, and it's simply not clear, in terms of a criminal judgement, what happened in regard to this specific issue or fact. And without labouring the point, it is, of course, no coincidence that the two verdicts open to you, in relation to any count on this document, in relation to any accused, is guilty or not guilty, that it's not guilty and innocent, and that, of course, is no coincidence. Now, some may think that these submissions are not at all attractive. I suspect some would say they're very unattractive in the extreme, because not only does it leave things in limbo, it leaves courts to be able to make findings that are most probably true but have not been proven to the requisite standard. This has all sorts of repercussions, repercussions to victims who are not getting the justice they deserve, political conditions considerations that we all know about. And to address this issue head on, and excuse me for saying it, it leads to men who are most probably guilty of extremely serious crimes actually walking free. Now, lest anyone think I am suggesting for one moment that that is the case with any of the accused in the dock in this case, I'm not. My submissions are entirely theoretical, but they apply equally to all cases at this Tribunal and to many other jurisdictions as well. And I've been at pains not to give any specific examples, save the mistakes of some of the advocates over the last few days. But I said a moment ago that these submissions are theoretical. They also happen to be true and central to the system of justice that you have been given the heavy responsibility of administering. It's a heavy burden you face, we suggest, in, among other things, dispensing appropriate justice, applying the burden of the standard of proof in the proper fashion. I started this -- the first section of my address by saying that I haven't made a closing speech for over four years. That may be true, but one thing I have proved to myself is that old habits do die hard, because I would never have had the guts and, some would say, be so foolhardy as to address a jury in this way, to look them in the eye and say what I have just said to you. We suggest that is the advantage of professional judges, and that advantage is the most important aspect of this criminal justice system and, we trust, it will be reflected both in your deliberations and your judgement. Now, moving on from that, I've already alluded to the impact what I've had to say has on witnesses. Assessing the credibility of witnesses is an essential part of your task. Obviously, the burden of standard of proof is vital here. I've already made some reference to it. If the Prosecution rely on an assertion or a piece of evidence of a witness, particularly if it's unsupported by any other piece of evidence, then you can only act upon it to the detriment of the accused if you're satisfied beyond reasonable doubt it's true and correct. As I've already said, the opposite isn't the case, and I won't repeat the point. Mr. Bourgon put the dilemma you face in this regard very well, we would suggest, at 34486, lines 4 to 15. In a trial such as the present one, the dilemma that he sets out is particularly acute, because a number of the witnesses whose credibility even the Prosecution question, the Prosecution have rightly cautioned you, both in their opening and in their final addresses, as to how some of the witnesses in this case need to be treated with great care. The Prosecution, as I've already pointed out, and I make no apology for saying so again, don't really remind the Trial Chamber how this isn't some sort of equal, level playing field when sizing up these witnesses; the Defence have the enormous advantage for the reasons I've already alluded to. Now a practical example of this, again, I believe Mr. Bourgon dealt with, and he's, to some extent, taken away my thunder, because he dealt with assertions or submissions made by Mr. Mitchell when he was dealing with Mr. Popovic's case at 34151, in relation to the Witness Acimovic. Now, obviously this witness had absolutely nothing to do with General Gvero's case, and again I'm just showing this as a good illustration of what I mean. The difficulty the Trial Chamber has with a witness such as Acimovic is to determine the facts from the fiction. The difficulty is all the greater when, if you're going to use what he says against an accused, you're going to have to be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that what he says is true, whereas the opposite, of course, is not the case. I've already made the point several times. Now, Mr. Mitchell, in fairness, goes on in his submission and makes some attempt to explain why Acimovic is reliable on the issue in question, and I'm not going to get into that, but it's a very rare -- perhaps the only example in this case of where my learned friend sitting on the other side of this courtroom have sought to help you in that way. They failed to do that lamentably. They leave you in a complete state of quandary as to how you're meant to size up the conflicting and contrasting interests of these particular witnesses. In this regard, I'd mention a further comment of Mr. Bourgon's, in fact on the same page of 34866. He said this: "We are confident that the Trial Chamber will have no difficulty in identifying the credible and reliable witnesses amongst them." Now, Your Honours, with the greatest respect, and I mean what I say, we have absolutely no doubt, that is, the Gvero Defence, that you will try your very best in this regard, but we do not really share Mr. Bourgon's confidence. It's not that we don't trust you, because the same point applies to all tribunals of fact, all courts, but the reality is it's often very difficult to discern when someone is telling the truth, when they're not, when they're lying, when they're trying to obfuscate. And it reminds me of a story. When I was a law student, part of my studies were trips to courts, and I remember going once with my group of fellow students to a court - I think it was a civil court, it wasn't even a criminal one. And when the litigants left, the rather elderly judge turned to us students and he said, "I was at the bar for 25 years and I've been on the Bench for 20 years, and what depresses me is after all this time I still cannot discern when someone is telling the truth." And it's a little anecdote, and excuse me if I'm giving evidence, but it's no more than stating the obvious, because it illustrates the difficulties we suggest you face, particularly in a case like this, when witnesses have so many differing motives for telling the truth, for lying, and something in between, as I've already said. Now, I've made some remarks a little earlier about professional judges and the advantage to an accused. One of those advantages is we are confident that when you say, in your judgement, We are satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that Witness A is telling the truth, that you will state why that is. We are satisfied this witness is truthful because of X, Y, and Z features. That way, an accused knows precisely why a piece of evidence about a particular witness or an assertion by a witness has been relied upon, and that particularly applies, of course, if you choose the testimony of a particular witness, the pick-and-choose method that the Prosecution are inviting you to embark upon in relation to so many of the witnesses they've called. Now, this has a particular application to one witness in the Gvero case, and that's General Milovanovic. Both the Prosecution and the Gvero Defence, in various parts of their brief, rely on him quite heavily. In paragraph 55 of their brief, the Prosecution say that Milovanovic "was evasive and less than candid" about Directive 4. Later on, they say that this document "would have incriminated him." And then they say his testimony "be regarded with great caution on this point." But the Prosecution brief elsewhere is literally peppered with references relying upon him. As far as we could make out, there were 61 such references as to where the Trial Chamber should rely upon what he was saying. And as I've already said, not a word from the Prosecution as to how you should weigh this out, how you should deal with this, why he's reliable in relation to these 61 references, but not in relation to Directive 4; nothing of any assistance to you in that regard. And, Your Honours, I'm going to say it once again, that the Defence can have it both ways in relation to this. The Defence are entitled to say, Yes, we -- if what he's saying may be true, some reasonable possibility it's true, we rely upon it, you act in the defendant's favour. If, on the other hand, it's adverse to the accused, it's got to be beyond reasonable doubt that it is true. We can have it both ways, and that's what we invite you to do when you come to deliberate. And General Milovanovic is pretty well like every Serb insider, to use that slightly ugly expression but one which conveniently allows us to know what type of witness we're talking about. We suggest all of these witnesses need to be treated, to use the Prosecution's words from paragraph 55 of their brief, "with great caution." In passing, I should say that the Prosecution pretty well did the same in their closing arguments. At 34060, they said he was unreliable, and on three occasions thereafter they rely upon him. But as I've already said, they don't help you at all as to how you should weigh this up, how you should deal with it. Now, to state the obvious, but I will very briefly, Milovanovic was, by common agreement, the second-most senior and powerful officer in the VRS. For reasons that some might find hard to fathom, he has avoided prosecution. He has every motivation to shift the blame, subtly or otherwise, to his subordinates, including Gvero. He has every motivation for obfuscation and basically avoiding the truth. Could I, before I leave this topic, mention one other thing. It's a slightly different point, but it's related. I'm not going to review other witnesses who fit into the same category, we suggest, as General Milovanovic, but when making your assessments of some of these other witnesses I have described as Serb insiders, please be very wary particularly in relation to some of the lengthy re-examinations or re-directs conducted in 2007 of their own witnesses by the Prosecution, and please bear in mind those re-examinations in the light of the Appeals Chamber decision of the 1st of February, 2008, titled "Decision on Appeals Against Decision on Impeachment of a Party's own Witness," where, to some extent, the procedure adopted by this Trial Chamber was said to be wrong by the Appeals Chamber. And bearing in mind those re-examinations were conducted under your guide-lines, just treat those passages with the utmost caution. We would suggest as well that the Prosecution had a deliberate policy of waiting and having these extremely long re-examinations, some of which went on for many, many hours, improper re-examinations - I accept you ruled against us so far as that's concerned - but that particular decision is important when you come to weigh up that evidence. Perhaps that would be a convenient moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honours, we'd now like to say a little bit -- another category of witness, witnesses I will describe as international witnesses. Now, of course, everything we've already submitted about other witnesses applies to international witnesses, but specifically in this regard Mr. Thayer, in his submissions, was at pains to defend somewhat passionately the honour and integrity of both Colonel Kingori and General Nicolai. I'm briefly going to deal with Kingori now, and Nicolai a little later, when I address the issue of the alleged threats to him. So far as Kingori is concerned, he, of course, again doesn't touch directly on my client's case, and in many ways, to the Gvero Defence, he's a witness of secondary importance. In the Defence brief, at page 156, paragraph 181, we make some robust submissions about the quality of his evidence. Mr. Thayer seeks to defend this gentleman's honour and courage. We say that's really neither here, nor there; it's his testimony that matters, and his testimony was, to put it kindly, of extremely poor quality. But, of course, that doesn't really take the matter that much further, because the issue again is: Can you rely upon what he says, so far as the Prosecution is concerned, beyond a reasonable doubt? And we submit the answer to that is emphatically: No. Now, we would invite you to look critically and carefully at international witnesses. They play an important part in Gvero's case. Because they were not, themselves, the warring parties - that may be putting it slightly inelegantly, but I'm sure you know what I mean - it doesn't mean that they must be truthful, let alone accurate. To raise them to some sort of higher strata of witnesses, as Mr. Thayer, in effect, seeks to do, is a mistake. As individuals, we contend that they are as prone to inaccuracy and exaggeration as any other human being, in particular in the highly stressful and emotional situations that these people found themselves in, in relation to the events surrounding this case. Furthermore, so far as this case is concerned, there is no getting away from the plain fact that there was, to put it mildly, a real motivation on the part of some of these international witnesses to down-play any moral culpability, perceived or real, by either themselves or other members of the international community that their actions or, more likely, inactions contributed even in some small way to the events that we've heard about over the last three years, and in particular, of course, the mass murder. Put simply, we suggest you need to examine the evidence of many of these witnesses with a highly-critical eye. We can put it no better than a quote that I put to Edward Joseph on the 24th of August, 2007, at the end of my cross-examination of 14262. The quote, in fact, in the transcript is slightly wrong, and the quotation comes from the book "Death of Yugoslavia," in the acknowledgment section of that book by Little and Silber, a highly-acclaimed account of the war. And what the author said there and what I put to Mr. Joseph was as follows: "To write any contemporary account of the Yugoslav wars is to navigate the thick waters not so much of deliberate dishonesty but of a contrived self-deceit. This applies not only to many of the combatants, but also, sadly, to those who came with good intentions to try to make peace." Your Honour, we echo those words and adopt them by way of comment about witnesses in this case, in general, and international witnesses in particular, and we suggest that they are sentiments and words well worth bearing in mind throughout your deliberations. I'm going to move on to a completely separate topic and, in a moment, deal with some errors that we allege in the Prosecution brief. But before I do that, on behalf of my team, let me hold my hands up and say we made a rather bad mistake in our brief, and I think Mr. Thayer had spotted it but was a gentleman enough not to mention it to you. Unfortunately, our paragraph numbering goes wrong. It starts again on at least two occasions. And so in order to refer to our brief, it's necessary to refer to the page number and the paragraph number. Mr. Thayer was good enough to do that, without drawing your attention to it. As I say, I've not actually spoken to him, but I suspect he spotted the point, and I'm grateful to his courtesy in that regard. So far as the Prosecution brief is concerned, they rely on 6D284, a document which was not admitted into evidence. That's at page 49, footnote 344 of their brief. It was put, in part, to Kosovac at T-30387, but wasn't actually tendered into evidence. Next, at paragraph 1754, footnote 4248, the Prosecution say that: "When Mladic and Milovanovic were away, people will report to Gvero." They cite in support of this Milovanovic, but what he actually said was that they would report to either General Djukic or General Gvero as the most senior members of the Main Staff when Mladic or Milovanovic were away. That's at 12305. Next, paragraph 1775, footnote 4295, the Prosecution have relied on the evidence of Skrbic to say that Mladic also knew that Gvero was at the Pribicevac IKM. Skrbic actually said 15619 the quote "General Mladic should have known" whether an assistant commander would go to an IKM. He did not say, in the particular instance, that he did, in fact, know whether Gvero went to that IKM at that time. Next, at paragraph 1801, the Prosecution state, in relation to Gvero's alleged order P45, the quote: "He took a direct role in the capture and detention of Muslim prisoners and personally branded the Muslims as inveterate criminals and villains." However, that's not a fair characterisation of that document, which of course the Defence suggest there's insufficient evidence to attribute to General Gvero in any event. What the document said was amongst them are -- let me correct that, let me get it right. Among them are inveterate criminals and villains. In passing, when dealing with that particular assertion in paragraph 10 -- 1801, the Prosecution say: "This order undoubtedly led to innumerable abuses by VRS soldiers against Muslims from the column." This, we suggest, Your Honours, is pure hyperbole, it's totally without support in the evidence, it's not a reasonable conclusion at all, let alone one proved beyond reasonable doubt. Our next point relates to paragraph 1806, footnote 4342: The Prosecution state that Tolimir's proposal, P192, and Mladic's final order, 5D-P35, also known but not admitted as P2897, of 13th of July, went -- the fact that it went to Gvero was not a fluke because it was wholly within Gvero's competencies, and in the paragraph I've just given they cite for this proposition Skrbic's testimony at 15616 to 15617, and they say: "General Skrbic testified that points 1 and 4 of Mladic's final order fell within Gvero's remit." This is, in fact, misleading, as Skrbic was only shown P192. He wasn't shown 5D-P35, which, as I've already said, is also the same as P2897. The point is that 1 and 4 of these two documents are completely different, they say completely different things. They've confused the tenor of Skrbic's testimony. The relevant bit I'm going to read to try and help unravel this confusion, the question was: "All right. And then you believe that under point 1, prohibiting access to all unauthorised individuals, filming and photographing of the prisoners, that parties would be General Gvero's task?" And Skrbic's reply was: "It falled under the sector led by General Gvero, but only this second part, filming and photographing prisoners, because the banning of all uninvited persons is something the military police were to perform." I hope that clarifies it. At paragraph 1807, footnote 4346, the Prosecution state that Tolimir addressed this new proposal to Gvero because he was the most senior general. They cite Milovanovic's testimony at 12368 in support. In fact, Milovanovic only said: "Probably, I think," because Gvero was the oldest officer -- the oldest general in the Main Staff. The next topic I'd like to briefly address, Your Honours, is something that I have alluded to before, I think, in oral submissions rather than written submissions, and that is the Appeals Chamber decision in the Prlic case of the 26th of February, 2009, titled "Presentation of Documents by the Prosecution in Cross-examination of Defence Witnesses." We suggest that this decision has clarified this particular subject, and had that decision been known at an earlier stage of this case, it would, we contend, significantly have affected the introduction of a large number of documents admitted on the application of the Prosecution post-98 bis. The reality is that the test that this Trial Chamber set down, in its decision of the 17th of December, 2008, is very different to the law as now set down and clarified by the Appeals Chamber. In the light of the Appeals Chamber decision, we contend that you must examine all material introduced by the Prosecution post-98 bis with the greatest of circumspection and, in particular, in the light of the test as laid down by the Appeals Chamber. And this leads on to another legal issue, which is that of notice. The Defence have complained, in their final brief, about the changing nature of the Prosecution case, both by way of pleading in the indictment and also by way of notice. This included Zepa and the shifting allegations as to General Gvero's alleged presence there dealt with at page 262 to 265 of the brief. Our basic point is: Why have a particularised indictment at all? Gvero's alleged contribution to the JCE is set out in paragraph 76. These were the areas the Defence needed to address. These are the areas, we suggest, of Gvero's alleged contribution that you need to determine in your judgement. The importance of this does not need stressing or explaining. The Defence asked rhetorically: What is the point of particularisation at all if the Prosecution case can chop, change, shift in the way that it has? We adopt what Madame Fauveau said so far as this topic is concerned, in particular her reliance on this Trial Chamber's own decision of the 31st of May, 2006, and, in effect, the failure by the Prosecution to abide by that particular decision. Perhaps I could move on and deal with this in a slightly more specific way, so far as some of the allegations that are now made against General Gvero that are of real significance. The first is so far as convoys are concerned. The Prosecution make much of Gvero's alleged role in restricting UN and humanitarian aid resupply convoys in paragraphs 217 to 218, 223, and 1765 to 1769 of their final brief. This allegation does not appear in the indictment. Whilst the Defence have to some degree addressed the Prosecution's vague pre-trial brief assertions as to Gvero's alleged role in restricting fuel to UNPROFOR at pages 188 to 193 of our brief, this in no way compensates for the prejudice now caused to the Defence by having no notice of a wider convoy and humanitarian aid allegations. If it was the Prosecution's case that Gvero contributed to the alleged JCE by assisting to restrict UN and humanitarian aid resupply convoys, then we suggest the law on this is abundantly clear from the Kupreskic appeal judgement, excuse me, at paragraphs 89 to 90. The acts and conduct of Gvero in allegedly restricting such convoys should have been specifically set out in paragraph 76 of the indictment. We note Mr. McCloskey's response at 34313 to a similar point raised in the Miletic Defence, and we contend this has no application to Gvero's case. This is because Mr. McCloskey pointed to paragraphs 50 to 54 of the indictment as particularised in the convoy allegations against Miletic in paragraph 75. Of course, we don't comment on whether or not paragraphs 50 to 54 do put Miletic on sufficient notice, which was also cross-referenced in paragraph 76. I beg your pardon. But they plainly do not provide sufficient specificity of the case against Gvero, as he's mentioned nowhere amongst them. In addition to that, we contend that Mr. McCloskey made no mention of the convoy allegations in his opening statement in relation to Gvero, which was something he relied upon when replying to Madame Fauveau's submission. We urge the Trial Chamber to entirely disregard the Prosecution brief as to Gvero's alleged role in restricting UN and humanitarian aid resupply convoys. This allegation has not been properly pleaded, and we have not been put on proper notice as to its existence; two separate points, I'm bound to say. A similar point arises so far as Directive 7 is concerned and what the Prosecution now say is an important issue; namely, Gvero's alleged attendance at the meeting in Bijeljina and Zvornik in 1992. We object to the Prosecution allegations, and I'm going to be specific here, in paragraphs 28 to 32 of the Prosecution's final brief, 56 to 61, 70 -- 1757 to 1763 and 1765, as well as their closing submission at 34051 and then a few pages later at 34056, as to Gvero's purported knowledge of and steps towards implementing the six strategic goals prior to the 8th of March, 1995. These allegations are absent from the indictment, the Prosecution pre-trial brief, as well as the Prosecution's opening statement. We submit this is an example of prejudicial surprise. The Defence, to flesh this out, if I may, objects to the Prosecution's use of these matters not as mere historical background utilised to place the material facts pleaded against Gvero in context, but rather their purported use by the Prosecution and allegations material to the common criminal objective of the JCE to forcibly transfer the Muslim populations of Srebrenica and Zepa. We suggest that the accused is entitled to proper particularity of the allegations in the indictment, and we also note that the Trial Chamber has the power to exclude evidence on the basis that the principles of fairness require due notice or uncertainty, and further support for this can be found in the case I've already cited, Kupreskic, 23rd of October, 2001, Appeals Chamber judgement at paragraph 92. Finally on this topic, the Defence also make a related but broader submission that any evidence related both to Gvero's attendance at and knowledge gleaned from the Bijeljina and Zvornik meetings, in addition to his knowledge of the six strategic goals and Directive 4, is relevant only for background and context to the charges in the indictment. This is because on any reading these matters fall temporally outside the scope of the indictment. For the avoidance of doubt, we contend this applies to paragraph 28 to 32, 56 to 61, 70, 1757 to 1762 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- of the Prosecutions final brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I heard the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- thanking you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters, and I'm grateful to Your Honours for bringing that to my attention. The earliest date --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you need to repeat the last part, referring to the para numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 28 to 32, 56 to 61, 70, as well as 1757 to 1762. The indictment clearly states that the earliest date upon which the common criminal objective of the JCE to forcibly transfer can come into existence is on the 8th of March, 1995. The Defence also view as instructive in this regard the fact that the only mention of the six strategic goals and Directive 4 is outlined in the indictment under a heading "Background," and that's at paragraphs 19 to 21 of the indictment. We submit that the Trial Chamber ought to limit its reliance upon such evidence to mere clarification of the background and context of the charges in the indictment, at the most. It would be improper to rely upon such evidence in order to establish the individual criminal responsibility of the accused. On a related but different point, Your Honours, we wish to draw your attention to what we regard as sweeping conclusions made by the Prosecution at the integral elements of the alleged JCE, which are simply unsubstantiated by evidence. We submit that the assertions that I'm about to refer to are conclusions which are critical to determining the individual responsibility of our client, that is, his knowledge of the alleged common criminal purpose of the JCE, and they indicate the dearth of evidence against him so far as the charges in the indictment are concerned. In particular, we refer to paragraph 1744, where the brief states: "From his position in the Main Staff since its inception, Gvero was fully informed of and actively participating in the RS and VRS policy to remove the Muslim civilian population from Eastern Bosnia, as set forth in the six strategic objectives and Directive 4 and 7." A similar point arises, so far as paragraph 1747 is concerned, where the Prosecution, I'm going to paraphrase, allege Gvero's responsibility to inform "the officers and troops of the important goals of the RS and VRS of separating the Muslim population from the Serbian population, and the reasons behind this goal." And, finally, paragraphs 1760, which deals with the discussions at Bijeljina and Zvornik, the Prosecution say: "There can be no doubt that Gvero has specific knowledge of the policy of ethnic cleansing, as set out in Directive 4." Now, the Gvero Defence, Your Honours, are between a rock and a hard place because we have made these complaints to you and we ask you to rule in our favour upon them, but nonetheless some of these issues have arisen. In particular, we suggest they've arisen very late in this case. And such evidence as there are, it may be will be against us, and we feel we'd be failing in our duty to our client not to address these issues. So notwithstanding our submissions as to lack of notice, the changing nature of the Prosecution case, the fact that much of this case, we suggest, is unsupported by admissible evidence, we take a belt-and-braces approach, and I'm going to pass the bat on to Mr. Krgovic, who is going to address you on some of the issues that I have just alluded to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours and distinguished colleagues. Your Honours, as my colleague Mr. Josse has just said, the question of General Gvero's part in the removal of the population of Eastern Bosnia was posed for the first time by the Prosecutor in his final brief, where, in detail, he presented accusations against him linked to this topic. With regard to the six strategic goals which the Prosecutor, in his final brief - transcript page 34050 - calls the gospel truth of ethnic separation, the position of the Defence is presented in the final brief on page 121, and we consider that the Trial Chamber in the Krajisnik trial made a reasonable ruling and determined that the strategic goals do not have an unlawful character, nor do they contain anything incriminating within them. Linked to those strategic goals, in paragraphs 1757 of their final brief, the Prosecutor mentions the meeting in Bijeljina in September 1992, which, according to the allegations of the Prosecution, was attended by General Gvero. Through the Prosecutor's interpretation of that particular meeting, the six strategic goals become the main topic of that meeting. However, Your Honours, that is just not true. If you look at the testimony of Witness Simic, for example - transcript page 28649 to 28651 - you will see that the purpose of that meeting was quite different, the conflict between paramilitary troops and the Army of Republika Srpska in Bijeljina, and the strategic goals are mentioned just in passing. So extracting that portion of the meeting, for which the Prosecutor has no evidence to show whether Gvero, in fact, took part, leads you to make the wrong conclusion, and that is whenever there is mention of those six strategic goals in any context, that that has to be the main topic and that the VRS has no better business to attend to but to discuss the subject of ethnic cleansing. Carrying on along the same lines through paragraph 1759 and 1760 of the Prosecution brief, the Prosecutor deals with the seminar in Zvornik and tries to link it up to Directive number 4. However, Your Honours, there is not a shred of evidence to show that that meeting had anything to do with Directive number 4. And if you look at the contents of the order for preparation of the military/political consultation in Zvornik, which is P4221 and P4222, you can see that nowhere is the topic of this seminar Directive number 4. Your Honours, Directive 4, as the witnesses has said, is a confidential document and represents a state secret. Witness Dragica Masal - transcript page T-29055 - spoke about the treatment of document which are labeled "State Secret," as is the case with Directive 4. The witness clearly sated that apart from the individuals who were directly included in the drafting of documents of this nature, nobody was allowed to know of the contents of those documents. The drafters of those documents are duty-bound to keep them secret. And with respect to their knowledge about the subjects of these documents -- treated in these documents, they had to keep them to themselves and were not allowed to disseminate. That is on transcript page T-29055. Bearing all this in mind, Your Honours, it would be highly unlikely and improbable that a large meeting of the type the meeting was in Zvornik, attended by many people from different social structures, civilians, soldiers, officers holding different ranks from different units, to openly discuss top-level state and military secrets. Furthermore, testifying on the 25th of February, 2009 - transcript page 32075 - Witness Pandurevic, when asked by the Prosecutor, responded and said that there was no mention of Directive 4 at that meeting, and no other witness confirmed that any directive was mentioned at all, nor did the Prosecution move evidence in that direction. For wont of a better, the argument that the Prosecution uses to establish a link is General Zivanovic's speech in which he mentions some duties and assignments with respect to certain built-up localities in Bosnia.
