However, this argument is insufficient because the duties and the settlements that are mentioned in General Zivanovic's speech do not coincide with the duties and localities mentioned in Directive 4. According to Exhibit P4402, Zivanovic mentioned the following places: Visnjica, Sapna, Teocak, Cerska, Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde. In order to contrive an artificial link with Directive 4, in which only four of these seven settlements are mentioned, the Prosecutor, in his brief, intentionally fails to mention the remaining three settlements. He just takes what suits him in order to make this link, which, when we look at the context of Zivanovic's entire sentence, leads us to doubt as to what was actually said at the seminar and discussed at the seminar in Zvornik. Anyway, the Prosecutor practically acknowledges the shortcomings in para 17660, and he says that in the presence of a number of individuals from the political and military leadership, the plans and goals from Directive 4 must have been discussed. It was in English "must have been discussed," which, Your Honours, the Defence would like to invite the Trial Chamber to see that this -- that the "beyond reasonable doubt" test has not been proved. Your Honours, looking at all this and bringing into -- and linking up these two meetings, the Prosecutor is contriving evidence, wanting to show that at that time there was a consciousness on the part of General Gvero. And I'd like to say that before this meeting in Bijeljina, General Gvero sends a letter on the 20th of June, in fact, 1992, which is 6D129, in which he cautions for the umpteenth time what kind of treatment the civilian population should receive in Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially those of different ethnicities. Now, if he's sending out this caution and warning people about this matter, he states his attitude, would he then discuss matters in this way about strategic goals in the sense that the Prosecution views this? So between these two events, on the 16th of October, 1992, General Gvero sends guide-lines for punishing the perpetrators of criminal acts to the military prosecutor. Does that mean that he's sending proposals to be found guilty, himself, if he refers to Directive 4 or the goals in that directive, which are questionable? In one way, he takes part in that; in another way, he proposes that he be sanctioned himself. Your Honours, I'm now going to deal with the alleged participation of General Gvero in the writing of Directive 7. Now, this accusation was first put forward in the Prosecution final brief, and this accusation, that General Gvero took part in the drafting of Directive 7, is not mentioned by the Prosecutor in the indictment or in the pre-trial brief or, indeed, in his opening statement. His position about this matter, the Prosecutor changes at the end of this trial, as my learned friend Mr. Josse said, that General Gvero must have taken part in the writing and drafting of that directive, because allegedly he used the full method, as it was called, in its elaboration. Now, this Court has heard a number of witnesses who testified about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the problem, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. The paragraph is 1765.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among these prosecutors [as interpreted], we have Petar Skrbic, Mirko Trbic, Nedeljko Trkulja, and Defence witnesses Ljubo Obradovic, Novica Simic, Ratko Miljanovic, and Slobodan Kosovac. However, even a superficial analysis -- let me repeat, for the record, the names of those witnesses. Petar Skrbic, Mirko Trbic, Nedeljko Trkulja, and Miletic's witnesses Ljubo Obradovic, Novica Simic, Ratko Miljanovic and Slobodan Kosovac. However, if a superficial analysis of their testimony brings into doubt the conclusion whereby all these witnesses are just -- well, these witnesses are making only theoretical comments on the general nature in which documents in the VRS were drafted, and according to their own acknowledgment, none of these witnesses in their military careers ever took part in the writing of a single directive, nor did they write a single directive. Therefore, none of these witnesses, when referring to directives in general, were not in a position to directly confirm -- personally confirm the joint thesis of the Miletic and Prosecutor's defence that Directive 7 was allegedly drafted by means of what was called the full method. First of all, Your Honours, from the title of Directive 7 itself, we see, without a doubt, that it is a directive of the Supreme Command, which leads us to a separate methodology in the elaboration of that document. With respect to the manner in which directives were written in general, the Prosecutor, in his final brief, paragraph 1672, wrongly interprets its own witness, Milovanovic, when he says that the assistants were consulted with respect to the drafting of the directive. However, Milovanovic, in his testimony, clearly states that when the guide-lines were given by the Supreme Command, then it is not indispensable and assistant commanders need not be consulted, which excludes the application of the so-called full method. And this is to be found on transcript 12274 to 12276 of the testimony. The only valid written piece of evidence as to how directives were written, including Directive 7, who provided the guide-lines and how the information necessary was collected, was 6D311. Those are bullet points proposed to the president of the Republika Srpska for the directive on special measures in the Eastern Bosnia Corps zone of responsibility. Witness Novica Simic first confirmed that those were the bullet points for Directive 7, and then following an objection from the Miletic Defence, he changed his answer. But the document speaks for itself. That's transcript page 28610. Your Honours, if the common position of the Prosecutor and the Miletic Defence on the application of the full method in the drafting of Directive 7 were correct, then the following two qualified witnesses would have, in view of their positions at the time, would have to be involved in the drafting of the directive. One is Witness Skrbic, assistant commander for personnel and mobilisation of the VRS Main Staff at the time of the drafting of Directive 7 and Directive 7.1. He says, however, that he had never seen Directive 7 before he was shown it by the Prosecution, even less had he participated in its drafting; transcript page 15517 and 15518. Witness Miljanovic, the assistant of General Djukic and assistant commander for logistics of the VRS Main Staff, said that in March 1995, he had not seen or participated in the drafting of Directive 7 and 7.1; transcript page 28957. Furthermore, Witness Obradovic and Witness Kosovac agree that the Directive 7, itself, does not contain any clues as to how the directive was written; transcript pages 30256 to 30258. Regardless of this, and attempting to confirm his theory on the so-called full method of drafting of Directive 7, the Prosecutor quotes part of the Miljenko Lasic evidence in paragraph 1765, where the witness speaks in very general terms on the work of the Command; also transcript page 28475. Ignoring this, as I said, the Prosecutor quotes part of the evidence of Miljenko Lasic concerning the work of the Command. There is no doubt that Witness Lasic was qualified to speak about this. From June 1992 until May 1993, he was assistant chief for operations and training at the VRS Main Staff; transcript page T-21723 and Exhibit P3178. Referring to Lasic, the Prosecutor deliberately avoids to comment on the other answers provided by the same witness regarding Directive 7 and Directive 4. Witness Lasic clearly says that he had no knowledge on how the directive was drafted; transcript pages 21807 and 21808. With reference to Directive 4, which was written at a time when the witness worked at the Main Staff, himself, Lasic clearly denies that the full method was applied. He testifies that Directive 4 was written by the chief of staff himself so that neither he, Lasic, although he was a member of the same staff and, ex officio, authorised to draft such documents, nor others were acquainted with any details from this directive; transcript page T-21829. Unlike the aforesaid witnesses, who had never participated in the drafting of directives themselves, this Court has also had two persons who personally wrote some of them. Prosecution Witness Milovanovic confirms that he personally drafted Directive 4; T-12195 and T-12199. The Miletic Defence witness Dragica Masal, an operations officer of the Main Staff, drafted Directive 9, describing it in his testimony as the result of the abridged method of work by the VRS commander, chief of the Main Staff of the VRS, and the witness, himself, as operations officer; T-29069. On transcript pages T-1295 says -- the Prosecution Witness Milovanovic says that he personally drafted a directive as chief of the Main Staff. Where are the full methods here, where is team-work, where is the participation of other people? Your Honours, these two witnesses confirm, in no uncertain terms, that only the person designated by the commander, usually the chief of staff, is the person who drafts the directive. All these theories about team-work in the Command are blown out of the water when we start discussing the coming into being of Directives 4 and 7, which are key issues in this case. Look, Your Honours, at evidence of General Djukic. You will see that what Djukic said about the writing of directives and the work of the staff is confirmed by Milovanovic and Dragisa Masal; Exhibit 6D313 and 6D315. The argument used by the Prosecutor, in corroboration of his theory about the full method and the implication of Gvero in the writing of Directive 7, is the fact that they include point 6.7, which bears the title "Moral and Psychological Support of Combat Activities." Insufficient, but the only argument that the Prosecutor has. According to the Miletic and Prosecution logic -- just one transcript correction. It was point 6.1. The contents of this paragraph would have to emanate, logically, from Gvero's organ for morale, religious and legal affairs. This argument is easily overturned by the testimony of Prosecution Witness Skrbic; T-15549, and Miletic's expert, Kosovac, T-30243 to 30426. Both these witnesses testified that apart from the heading, no part of this paragraph falls into the remit of the organ for morale, nor was it written by a qualified and trained military person, which General Gvero certainly was according to the compliment he received from the Prosecutor that he was qualified and trained for his job. Your Honours, not only is there no evidence in this case to show that General Gvero participated in the writing of Directive 7, there is equally no evidence that he was ever acquainted with it. Let me go back for a moment -- Your Honours, I'm sorry, there's an interpretation issue. Just a moment What I said was that there is no evidence that General Gvero was acquainted with Directive 7. Let me go back for a moment to the evidence of Skrbic and Miljanovic on another important point. Both these witnesses, members of the Main Staff, testify that they had not seen either Directive 7 or Directive 7.1. The evidence of Masal and Obradovic will assist us in understanding how it was possible that two members of the Main Staff had never seen such an important document. As I said, speaking about the meeting in Zvornik, Witness Masal - transcript page 29055 - speaks about documents marked "state secret" or constitute a state secret, as was the case with Directives 4 and 7, and he explains that save for the persons directly involved in the drafting of such documents, no one else should know anything about their contents. Witness Obradovic explains that Directive number 7 was kept in a special safe box; transcript 28343. Furthermore, Witness Masal explains that anyone and everyone involved in the writing of a directive must sign it to confirm their participation in the drafting or to indicate authorship. If the joint theory of the Prosecution and the Miletic Defence is that the directive was drafted by the Main Staff, why -- there is no indication that it was a product of the Main Staff. To put it briefly, it has not been proven beyond a reasonable doubt that Milan Gvero participated in the drafting of Directive 7. As far as the role of General Gvero in the restriction of humanitarian aid is concerned, it is not superfluous for me, I believe, Your Honours, that Milan Gvero was not charged with restricting humanitarian aid. However, the Prosecution trial brief is full of allegations in this regard. Let us start in chronological order. The Prosecution invokes two documents from December 1994, that is, outside the context and the time of the indictment, trying to show as evidence of Gvero's alleged participation in authorising convoys of humanitarian aid, although the said documents have absolutely nothing to do either with the convoys or with the humanitarian aid. Documents P4153 and P4152, Your Honours, speak of individuals and vehicles crossing the state border between Republika Srpska and Yugoslavia; that is to say, the route from Belgrade to Sarajevo, Zvornik, Bratunac, and Srebrenica, Banja Koviljaca, and Republika Srpska. In both these cases, we're dealing with information about the crossing of state borders by individuals and not goods. There are no humanitarian convoys, no humanitarian aid, or humanitarian goods. Paragraph 1767 of the Prosecutor's final brief once again implies the restriction of humanitarian assistance, once again unfounded. When Witness Kralj explained -- expounded on a Prosecution exhibit, and the number was P4036, he explained, in response to my question, what this document was about, because the Prosecutor had pulled it out of context. And that is on transcript page 29378 and 29379. And here they were discussing meetings of the commission for the implementation of the peace agreement. I should like to remind Your Honours of the testimony of Witness Kralj from that portion of the transcript, where General Gvero -- saying that General Gvero was a member of the commission for the implementation of the peace agreement in Bosnia-Herzegovina from December 1994 to the end of April 1995, except in March 1995 when, because of an injury during a traffic accident, he was absent from the Main Staff and was not performing his duties there. And that is on page T-24099 of the transcript. All the activities of General Gvero, as a member of the said commission, evolved during this particular period of time. At that time, during that period, that is to say, from December to April 1994, with the exception of the month of March, you will see that his name was mentioned in connection with these activities. When the Muslim side, at the end of April 1995, as is common knowledge, in a unilateral way interrupted the agreement on a cease-fire, the peace agreement was cut short and, therefore, General Gvero's activities in that regard. In our final brief, we deal in part with the meetings. However, I'd like to remind you of Prosecution Exhibit P2936, page 2, item 7, and the agenda there. In his final brief, the Prosecutor, when questioning General Smith, he depicted the meeting as saying that Gvero had come and talked about humanitarian aid, but just take a look at the agenda, point number 1, the continuation or prolongation or extension of the agreement on a cease-fire, a cessation of hostilities. Just one sentence by General Gvero pulled out of context after the official part of the meeting was over, and that helps the Prosecutor to try to show that Gvero was implicated in the context of restricting humanitarian aid. As a member of that commission, General Gvero attended various meetings linked to the implementation of the peace agreement, and at these meetings, Your Honours, meetings were agreed upon for regional commissions in places throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is Exhibit 5D1418. In an attempt to depict General Gvero and to strike a link between him and the restrictions on the humanitarian aid convoys, the Prosecutor tries, by a handwritten addition on documents, to tie in Gvero and his authority with respect to limiting and restricting those convoys. Now, if you look at that document, itself, Your Honours, P4316, you will see that the individual who has written in the portion and does not know what the meeting was about, because they weren't present, is simply seeking information from members of the commission in order to learn whether what it says in the document was actually agreed at the commission meeting. So it's not consultation; it's seeking information about whether this subject was discussed by the commission at its meeting or not. Furthermore, paragraph 1768 of the Prosecution's final brief attempts, yet again, to prove that Gvero knew and that he received various documents linked to the convoy. Especially paragraph 1767 is characteristically contradictory. The Prosecutor accepts the fact that Witness Kralj could not identify the initials on document P4036. However, he nonetheless says that General Gvero did initial the document, as well as the following documents, P4028, P4015, P4039, P3999, and P4040. The Prosecutor tried to link this up by comparing the said initials on P4036 with another, as he says, characteristic set of initials on a document dating back to 1992 and linked to the treatment of civilians and journalists, and that is 6D129, and another document from 1995, which concerns a peace mission. Let's stay with 6D129 for a moment. From the text of this document itself, you will see that it is a document which Gvero compiled and sent to the corps. 6D129 is a copy which was received in one of the corps via a teletype, so they received a telegram, in actual fact. It would be completely unnecessary and illogical for General Gvero to send this document to the corps from the Main Staff and that somebody received it in a corps and then confirmed, by initialling it, its reception, the reception of his own document. We wish to emphasise at this point that it is absolutely inadmissible for the Prosecution to attempt, in this way, to link General Gvero to the mentioned documents. If the Prosecutor wanted to prove and show General Gvero's participation through his initials, then he should have and could have done this during the long trial by calling in an expert -- handwriting expert, who would professionally analyse Gvero's handwriting and make his own conclusions on that. The Prosecution deliberately failed to do that, and not only that, the Prosecutor had every opportunity, during the examination of Witness Kralj, to directly put it to the witness that in this specific case it was, in fact, Gvero's signature, which, Your Honours, was the objection I raised at the time, and there was the suggestion by the President of this Trial Chamber that followed. The Prosecutor once again chose not to act upon it. And this is on page 29346 of the transcript. With an absence of compelling evidence, the Prosecutor is guessing and saying that the initials belong to General Gvero. That is insufficient, because at the very least there is reasonable doubt as to who those initials, termed characteristic initials, actually are. Your Honours, to link up General Gvero's participation in the work of the commission for the implementation of the peace agreement and to approve humanitarian aid, absolutely -- are not absolutely interconnected, because what would that standard of proof be? It would mean somebody is guilty for trying to implement a peace agreement which is trying to achieve peace. Is that guilt, is that blame? Your Honours, I will end there. Those are the facts set forward by me with respect to the Prosecutor's allegations, and my colleague will continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry about that. I'm just trying to make the conditions in the courtroom more comfortable, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure I, being on my feet, particularly appreciate that. Thank you, Your Honours. I'm sure the Registrar will deduct that from our time. Your Honours, there's only one other topic that I'm going to deal with in any detail at all, and then there are a few I'm going to deal with absolutely in passing. The topic in a little bit of detail is dealt with at paragraph 282, page 204 of the Defence brief, and there we say the following: "The Defence say, as a starting point, that Milan Gvero did not say that he would have the compound at Potocari and the surrounding areas shelled. Of this, all concerned can be sure." Well, Your Honours, the Defence was wrong about that, because the Prosecution's final brief on this very issue begins by continuing to peddle this patently incorrect line, and that's at paragraph 1781. It was wrong because, fortunately for Gvero, the Muslims had intercepted this conversation and recorded it verbatim. That's P2374. And the plain fact of the matter is Gvero simply did not say what Nicolai alleged and what, extraordinarily, the Prosecution continue to allege in their brief. It's almost as if they hadn't read the cross-examination of that witness. Now, Your Honours, the Prosecution go on in their brief and seek to justify this by quoting from Nicolai's Assen debriefing note of the 18th of September, 1995. And as a very minor aside, the quote at footnote 4309 is in evidence, but the actual document at footnote 4308 is actually not in evidence. And the same applies to footnote 4306. But getting back to the substantive point, the use by the Prosecution of this debriefing quote is hopeless. I repeat what I have said. We know, from the transcript of P2374, that Gvero did not say what's alleged in the debriefing note. The debriefing note reads: "Bombing the stream of refugees, the Potocari compound." The fact that Nicolai was wrong about this so soon after the event only goes to show how mistaken and unreliable he is. And it was demonstrated to him, as I've already mentioned, in cross-examination that he was wrong. And I've already said, and I make no apology for repeating it, it's nothing short of bizarre that the Prosecution should continue with this line. We go on and say that this is highly illustrative of the very thing that Mr. Thayer, in his closing arguments, alleged the Defence of falsely accusing General Nicolai of; namely, bias. Now, it's either that or extreme confusion, or both. You've heard me make some submissions about international witnesses. What I would say about General Nicolai is in response to Mr. Thayer's argument at 34080, when he took exception to what he called "an absolutely baseless personal attack" on Nicolai. He claims there's no evidence of partiality on Nicolai's part. Well, we suggest that the error just alluded to makes that, at the very least, a possibility. But Mr. Thayer's defence of General Nicolai is really somewhat extraordinary when one contrasts what General Nicolai said and what Mr. Thayer says in his support with what General Smith said. And let's remember, General Smith was Nicolai's direct superior. Nicolai was his chief of staff. And General Smith's whole attitude and enmity towards the Bosnian Serb leadership was something he really accepted, you may think. For example, he said in evidence that he wasn't prepared to negotiate with Mladic in June of 1995, whereas Janvier was, for example. He accepted extracts from his, Smith's, book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was, for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: General Janvier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Janvier, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He accepted, this is General Smith, extracts from his book put to him, 6D186, where he said in terms that he was at war -- or perhaps I should say he was effectively at war with Mladic, and that's at 17749 of the transcript. And you won't forget the quotation from Fortin's diary, the entry of the 10th of July, 6D165, which was dealt with in private session and I won't repeat, which is at 17785 to 86 of the transcript. When you bear that in mind and what General Nicolai's superior was saying, is Mr. Thayer seriously saying that there isn't the remotest possibility -- there's only a remotest reasonable possibility, that General Nicolai was a tad bit biased, that he didn't quite perceive things in the clean way that Mr. Thayer alleges? Please bear that in mind when you come to weigh up General Nicolai's evidence. Now, whilst on the subject of the alleged threat, we submit as follows: The Prosecution rely at 34079 on Nicolai's testimony that it was Gvero's threat that made them decide to stop the air-strikes. We suggest there's clear evidence leading to a reasonable doubt on the issue. That's contained in our brief at page 205, paragraph 286, and in particular it relates to Fortin's testimony that the air-strikes were suspended as a result of the VRS threat at 1400 hours read over the radio by the captured NCO. It's also pages 205 to 206 of our brief, paragraph 287 to 289, that it was a Karaman threat that led to the cessation of air-strikes and that he couldn't recall with certainty whether or not the threat was transmitted by Gvero. In the absence of certainty, we suggest, from the Prosecution's main witness, any doubt must be accorded to the accused. Then at 34079, we have Mr. Thayer again asserting "he had to know," and this was in the context of other threats. We suggest this is pure speculation based on no evidence whatsoever, it's rhetoric of the worst kind, and, indeed, highly prejudicial and quite improper coming from a prosecutor. Now, Your Honours, the Prosecution themselves acknowledge at 34079, over to the next page, that by the time of the second conversation, the one with General Gobillard, the air-strikes had already been suspended. By this admission, we suggest that they are accepting that Gvero's second conversation couldn't amount to any kind of effective threat against Gobillard leading to decisive action on the air-strike issue, as UNPROFOR had already made up their minds by the time of that discussion. And, Your Honours, at paragraphs 280 to 281, pages 202 and 203 of our brief, you'll see our assertion that the Prosecution case on this issue has also changed. The case, as opened, and, in particular, as indicted, where they only talk about a singular commander, was a threat against Nicolai, not against Gobillard. Don't let them get away with it, we suggest. They simply can't chop and change their case in this way. A related but slightly different topic is the warning that General Gvero sent to the Drina Corps immediately after these conversations on the 11th of July, which is 6D207. Both parties have set out their positions in their briefs, and Mr. Thayer mentioned it in his address. We suggest to you that the Prosecution case, so far as this document is concerned, is that black is really white. They say that Gvero clearly doesn't mean what he says in that document. Well, of course, it's very easy for them to say that, but it's very difficult to prove, and it's something they have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt. We suggest they haven't got near doing that. Of course, what Mr. Thayer fails to address in his rhetoric to you is their very own expert on this particular subject, because Mr. McCloskey asked Mr. Butler about this document, and this is what Mr. Butler said, I quote: "This is a fair example of a good military idea that was overcome by events." That was at 19801, and Mr. Butler confirmed that again in cross-examination at 20722. Your Honours, a good military idea. How on earth can that be criminal and multifarious, as Mr. Thayer alleges in his submissions to you. Now, Madame Fauveau referred to this document today in her submissions, contrasting it to the alleged Gvero order, P45. She described 6D207 as an order. We submit that that's an incorrect description of the document, and that is one of the ways one can contrast P45 to 6D207. Our full submissions as to P45, of course, can be found in our brief at pages 216 to 221. I digress slightly to deal with that. One other thing I'd like to deal with, whilst on a related topic, and that was something that Mr. Thayer ended with, and that was an intercept between Gvero and a man called Subara, P1134, which was dealt with at page 134, paragraph 39 of our brief, and we say there is some similarity between that and 6D207, not in terms of the intercept and the document, but in the way the Prosecution approached them. They simply say, and I make no apology for using the same phraseology, that black is white, and they can't give you any reason as to why black is white. They simply throw mud, and that's what it is, mud at General Gvero, and they hope it's going to stick. And, of course, they have to say that, because otherwise their case simply doesn't add up and doesn't make sense. And bearing in mind the burden of standard of proof, we are sure you'll have no difficulty in rejecting that sort of approach from the Prosecution. Now, Your Honours, I'm going to go through a few more issues much more briefly. I think there's one I can deal with before the break, and that is the alleged intercept between General Gvero and Radovan Karadzic. This was dealt with in closing at 34082, and the Prosecution complained that the transcripts that we were relying upon do not mention -- they complain that we have falsely portrayed 6D14 and 6D15, the transcripts we refer to, in our brief. Your Honour, the Trial Chamber can feel confident upon the accuracy of the contents of those transcripts. They were played in full to the relevant witness, PW-145, during his testimony, and he explicitly confirmed at 7264 that their contents are identical to the conversations in the intercepts. Now, as such, although only Gvero's side of the conversation has been recorded and, therefore, it's only his part of the conversation that appears on the transcript, it's very clear that the record of the call commences from the beginning and also includes the portion of the conversation with the operator. As such, you can feel confident and, indeed, able to verify independently that nowhere in those intercepts is the name Karadzic mentioned either by the participants during the conversation --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: My apologies. You can feel confident that nowhere in those intercepts is the name Karadzic mentioned either by the participants during the conversation or by the operator at the beginning of the call. We suggest, as set out in our brief at pages 193 to 202, that PW-145's purported identification of Karadzic as the other participant in that conversation, and the fact that it appears in the headers of P1096 and P2375, the transcripts the Prosecution rely upon, is or may be based on a series of mistaken assumptions and cannot be relied upon beyond reasonable doubt. Significantly, PW-145 admitted during his live testimony that he could not be sure of the participants in the conversation. Briefly on this topic, at 34083, Mr. Thayer characterised one of these discussions - I think it was P1096 - as short, curt and polite, and he said that this establishes that is a call with Karadzic, somebody with whom he has -- I haven't got the quote here, but Your Honour has the page reference. We submit that Skrbic's evidence is diametrically opposite to the assertion made by Mr. Thayer. Skrbic described the call as a friendly exchange and was symptomatic of a "relationship full of respect." And that's set out in our brief at paragraph 261, pages 193-4. We say that couldn't apply to a conversation between Gvero and Karadzic for reasons the Trial Chamber are well aware of. With Your Honours' leave, perhaps we could take the second break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a break of 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next topic, Your Honours, is the meetings of the 22nd and 25th of August, dealt with by Mr. Thayer at 34076, where he deals with what he says is an incorrect citation in our brief at page 110. Could we concede that, unfortunately, in our brief we have mixed the two meetings up? As far as I could gather, Mr. Thayer had appreciated that, because he, in his submissions, addressed each meeting in the correct manner. It's the meeting on the 22nd of August which Gvero did not attend at Borike which was variously regarded by Smith as "fascinating," "a success," and "a step in the right direction." Contrast that, we say, with the meeting on the 25th of August, 1995, where Gvero didn't attend and which Smith regarded as "brief and businesslike." We next want to turn to paragraph 159 of the Prosecution brief, where they deal with General Gvero's alleged monitoring of Spreca 95. They say he monitored this operation by placing an assistant commander for morale at the forward command post. We contend that this shows a failure on the part of the Prosecution to understand the strict reporting structure within the VRS under which morale officers at the corps level did not and were not permitted to report directly to General Gvero's organ at the Main Staff level. This is dealt with in our final brief at pages 121/123, which describes how matters worked. In short, the Operations Department would receive reports sent from the corps commander. The Operations Department would then separate out the issues pertaining to the remit of the sector of each of the assistant commanders in the Main Staff. General Gvero would only have received updates as to the morale situation within the Spreca 95 operation through this channel. He would never have had any better insight into or influence over the operation resulting from a direct reporting line with the corps-level morale officer who was ordered by Mladic to be embedded at the forward command post, as set out in 5D-P2891, in short a complete misconception of the evidence by the Prosecution. Turning next to the issue of propaganda. Yet again, the allegation now made by the Prosecution that Gvero was the chief propagandist of the VRS does not appear in the indictment. Indeed, the Trial Chamber are invited to contrast this with paragraph 74(D)(1) in the indictment, where it says that Tolimir is "organised and led the psychological and propaganda activities related to the operations in Srebrenica and Zepa." We accept that in paragraph 277 of their pre-trial brief, the Prosecution asserted "Gvero was head of the department responsible for" inter alia, and then quote again "psychological and propaganda-related activities," but that allegation does not appear anywhere in the indictment and, as I've already said, it is levelled against Tolimir in the way that I've described. The extent to which we say General Gvero had some responsibility for these matters, they're dealt with in our brief at pages 94 to 98. In paragraph 161 of the Prosecution's brief, the Prosecution have erroneously conflated the Morale Sector's Information Service which was overseen by General Gvero and produced "Srpska Vojska" and the Centre for Information, Psychological, and Propaganda Activities, which was headed by Milutinovic and was directly subordinated to Mladic. These two units, we contend, were completely separate entities, and the latter was not overseen at all by our client and was, instead, directly subordinated to Mladic. Simic's evidence with regard to this is relied upon at page 113 of our brief. The Prosecution make the same error in the second paragraph of 1750 of their brief. In support of their assertion there, they cite Trkulja for this proposition at 15140, but in fact the witness only confirmed that General Gvero was in charge of "an information centre." He did not clarify which one or who it was headed by. In fact, when we were looking at this for the last time very recently, it became apparent that the proposition in the first sentence of paragraph 1750, where it says "another component of Gvero's role as chief propagandist of the VRS was to remain attuned to how the VRS was perceived in the international media, looking for opportunity to present the VRS positively, as well as watching out for sources of negative portrayal," the Prosecution only use a 1992 request of General Gvero's as the proper treatment of journalists at 6D129, and we say it's a quantum leap for the misleading proposition in the second sentence. It's an example of how one needs to read and analyse these Prosecution assertions very carefully. In fact, they cite no evidence at all in support of their rather startling proposition that Gvero's man was at the Hotel Fontana meeting. We ask, rhetorically, has that ever been an issue in this case? Have they ever said that Gvero had his man there at the Hotel Fontana? Of course not. Your Honours, they're making it up as they go along. The final example I'll give you of Prosecution's confusion between Tolimir, Gvero, and Miletic's responsibility for propaganda can be seen in 162 of their brief. They cite -- or, I beg your pardon, they state: "An example of psychological and propaganda activities of Gvero's organ directed against the enemy population with a loud-speaker used in Zepa to broadcast messages from General Mladic, calling on the Zepa population to leave the enclave." In fact, they erroneously cite P2588 for this proposition. It's a typographical error we accept, because they must mean it's P2788. However, the document in question is a direction from Tolimir to the Security Department of the 1st Krajina Corps. It refers to the involvement of the Milutinovic's centre, the one I have referred to earlier, being allowed in arranging with the Zepa loud-speaker. It has nothing whatsoever to do with General Gvero. At 34086, the Prosecution asserted, in their closing arguments, that Gvero had the ability to disagree with Mladic, whilst at the same time keep his job, and that this proves that Mladic trusted and valued Gvero. The relationship between these two men is fully dealt with in our final brief at page 77 onwards. In fact, we suggest, at the very least, the evidence in this case gives rise to an inference that Mladic had little option but to retain the devil he knew, rather than the SDS lackey that Karadzic clearly wanted to put in his place for Gvero's job, Deronjic in particular. In support of this proposition, we invite you to look at Simic's evidence 28 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. We rely on Simic's evidence, 28607; Skrbic, 15562; and Djukic's 92 quater statement, 6D315. Two legal issues. The first is the mass murder, Your Honours. Madame Fauveau has addressed the issue, and I'm going to do the same briefly. At various points of their final brief, the Prosecution make a bare assertion that General Gvero had knowledge of the mass murder operation; for example, paragraph 477 of their brief. They cite no evidence whatsoever in support of such a startling conclusion. This unsubstantiated submission cannot be accorded any weight whatsoever and sheds no light at all on Gvero's knowledge or mens rea in respect of the crimes for which he's charged in the indictment. Other examples of the same can be found in paragraphs 1804 and 1809. Your Honours, in short, this sort of stuff is the worst sort of prejudice. It fills no legitimate purpose, but it's much worse than that; it is totally illegitimate. It's totally illegitimate because, as the Prosecution well know, General Gvero is not charged with these allegations. They've chosen not to charge him with those allegations, and they are allegations which, I might add and to state the obvious, that are about as serious as one could possibly imagine and find anywhere amongst criminal offences. Your Honours, since he was not charged with these allegations, the Defence have at no stage in this trial sought to deal with them. That's what happens in criminal trials. The Defence seek to defend those matters with which their client is charged; nothing more and nothing less. Please bear that in mind. The last legal matter I wish to turn to is opportunistic killings. At 34174, Mr. Elderkin sought to deal with the Defence submission in relation to paragraph 31.1(A) of the indictment. What emerged from his submissions, as we understand it, is that the Prosecution are now saying that the alleged killings in question took place on the 13th of July, as opposed to the pleaded date of the 12th of July. The simple point is, and it's quite clear from the Gvero brief, that the issue that the Defence addressed, both in evidence and in the brief, was the case as indicted; namely, the 12th of July. We contend that it's both unfair and impermissible for the Prosecution to seek to change their claims in this way in their closing arguments. They didn't even do it in their final brief. And we rely in support of that proposition the case of Kunarac, judgement 4th of November, 1999, paragraphs 16 and 17. More generally on opportunistic killings, I'd like to make some submissions about foreseeability. The indictment alleges that the killings were a natural and foreseeable consequence of the JCE to forcibly transfer the population of Srebrenica. The Prosecution has pleaded no material fact in support of this allegation, merely providing details of the killings, themselves. The Defence, we contend, has had no indication of what information should have placed our client and his lawyers on notice that killings were a "natural and foreseeable consequence" of the displacements. On this basis alone, Counts 4 and 5 should be dismissed, as the material facts essential to this allegation have simply not been pleaded. Moreover, we contend, no evidence has been adduced during the course of this lengthy trial to indicate that the executions in question were a natural and foreseeable consequence of the evacuation of the civilian population from Srebrenica. The killings were entirely unconnected with the evacuation and, in fact, actually were or may have formed part of the JCE to mass murder the able-bodied men from Srebrenica, the burden in that regard, of course, being on the Prosecution. As explained in the Defence final briefs at pages 35 to 37, the Prosecution are required to prove beyond reasonable doubt that each of the separate allegations of opportunistic killing did not form part of the mass killings. At 34178, the Prosecution, in their submissions, asserted that the executions charged as opportunistic killings in paragraph 31 of the indictment were either "spontaneous acts of violence or targeted revenge," which "took place at locations other than the chosen execution sites and for reasons other than military orders." He said that it's this: "Opportunistic and foreseeable" character which distinguishes them from the "vast and organised mass killings," which were not foreseeable as a consequence of the forcible removal JCE. We contend that this submission holds no water in the light of paragraph 32 of the indictment, which relates to the summary executions of 16 men by a small squad of soldiers on an isolated bank of the Jadar River on the 13th of January, 1995. That allegation is plainly the same tenor as those alleged in paragraph 31 in the indictment and only indicates the sameness of the mass killing operation and the killings alleged to have been carried out opportunistically by the Prosecution. Even more importantly, we contend for our client's case, there is a complete lack of evidence indicating that General Gvero willingly accepted the risk of opportunistic killings taking place. His Honour Judge Kwon asked this very question to Mr. McCloskey last Friday at 34284. We suggest that our learned friend, Mr. McCloskey, was simply unable to point to any evidence to indicate Gvero's adoption of the risk at all. The dearth of evidence on this issue was such that he was forced to rhetoric about the ugliness of ethnic cleansing in wars and that VRS soldiers were going to act out against Muslims in the light of ethnic cleansing of Serbs from Grahovo and Glamoc. As discussed in relation to the foreseeability limb of the mens rea requirement for JCE 3, a general knowledge of a desire for revenge by some VRS soldiers or the possibility of war crimes being committed during a war is manifestly insufficient to show a willingness to accept the risk of opportunistic killings. Mr. McCloskey then purported to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- rely upon P2753, that's 2753, the document issued by General Gvero on the 10th of July, entitled "The Muslim War Trump Card." He said this in some way indicates Gvero's acceptance of the risk of opportunistic killings following on from the evacuation of the civilian population. Given that the evacuation operation had not yet taken place at the time that P2753 had been written, it's hard to see how this document could possibly indicate General Gvero's mens rea for the opportunistic killings of JCE 3. We contend that the Prosecution case on these killings is, to put it plainly, unsustainable. Your Honours, there's one final part of my address. I think it will take about 15 minutes. I'll certainly be finished well before the end of the day. I think I need to request five or ten minutes extra time, therefore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Absolutely no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, that would basically leave us with a few minutes before we are due to adjourn. I suppose you would prefer to start on Monday, won't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I would have started with anything up to 15 minutes left of the day, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There won't be 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I wish to turn to the issue of sentence, Your Honour. From the Defence's point of view, the decision by this institution to roll the conviction and sentence stage into one is unfortunate in the extreme. There are a number of difficulties and down-sides in this, and you'll be glad to know I'm not going to go into them all today. But from a Defence advocate's point of view, it places him or her in an invidious position. Throughout this trial, as we all know, in excess of three years, lawyer has been proclaiming from the roof-tops the innocence of his or her clients, and then right at the end of the procedure the lawyer has to say, Well, hang on a minute, Your Honours. If you happen to find my client guilty, then you might want to hear the following and bear it in mind when you come to sentence him. This, as I've already said, is highly unsatisfactory from the lawyer's point of view, but also from an accused's. But, in fact, it goes further than this, because in reality it makes it impossible for counsel to comment and mitigate on the exact basis on which his or her client has been convicted. By this, I mean as follows: If the procedure was, as we say it should be, judgement on conviction first, then this would allow an accused and his or her lawyers to know which counts the accused has been convicted of, and also in a judge-only system, such as is operative here, the accused would know the basis on which he's been convicted, the degree of culpability, because that would all be set down in the judgement. This would, in turn, allow the Defence advocate to address all these issues in mitigation prior to sentencing. Well, obviously, I cannot do that on behalf of General Gvero. The best I can do in this regard is to urge you that in the event of a conviction on any of the counts of this indictment, is for you, before you come to pass sentence, to replace yourself in the position that I'm in today and ask yourselves, What would the Defence be submitting at this juncture as to the nature of conviction, the degree of culpability, and what can be said on behalf of the accused in that regard? In relation to those matters that I can say at this junction, everything I say in the next few minutes needs to be considered in the context that Mr. Krgovic and I, on behalf of General Gvero, do not resile from the position we have advocated throughout this trial; namely, that our client is not guilty and the proper verdicts you should return in relation to all counts on this indictment is precisely that, not guilty. We say the Prosecution have not proved his guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. Addressing the issue as best I can, first and foremost, we contend that the Prosecution final brief's sentencing recommendation, so far as General Gvero is concerned, bears no relationship to reality. So far as General Gvero is concerned, deliberately or otherwise, it continuously falls into the same trap. The very first paragraph, 2806, says: "Over 7.000 people were systematically murdered." Now, without being blase about this important topic and whether this is true or not, there is no doubt that the terrible crime of mass murder was committed. There is also no doubt that Milan Gvero is not charged with this crime and is obviously not going to be punished for it at all. If the tarring of Milan Gvero with the brush of mass murder, in the context of sentencing, is a mistake by the Prosecution, it's careless and unfortunate in the extreme. If it's deliberate, it's nothing short of disgraceful. As for the recommendation, as I've already contended, it bears no relationship to reality. It is acknowledged by many commentators that sentencing at the ICTY is rather too much of an imprecise science. Now, there may be good reasons for this, but when it comes to Srebrenica-related offences, consistency, we suggest, is both possible and desirable because of the number of accused who've already been sentenced for their roles in these events. In this regard, we would invite Your Honours to examine certain passages from the very last judgement in relation to these events; namely, the Appeals Chamber judgement of Blagojevic and Jokic on the 9th of May of 2007. The topic, as a whole, is dealt with in paragraphs 319 to 346. In paragraph 332, the Appeals Chamber described the Prosecution's assertion that Blagojevic's sentence was inadequate compared to Krstic, Momir Nikolic, and that of Obrenovic. It's worth remembering that it was there that the Prosecution were arguing strongly for consistency and comparison. That's what they were urging on the Appeals Chamber. Now, it's true to say that at paragraph 333, the Appeals Chamber sets out the limited value of comparing sentences at this Tribunal. However, we contend that in paragraph 334, in reality, the Appeals Chamber do just that and do compare the sentences, because obviously the crime base is either the same or ostensibly the same, but the actual role of each of the accused in the crimes was different. And, for example, at the very end of that paragraph, the Appeals Chamber says, and I quote: "Blagojevic's criminal liability is also distinguishable because, unlike Momir Nikolic and Dragan Obrenovic, Blagojevic was not convicted of participating in the mass killing operation." The position and analysis, we contend, is similar at paragraph 345 so far as Jokic is concerned. It's clear, from what I have just read out, that comparing Srebrenica offenders is a validity. Now, of course, at the same time, that a Trial Chamber, in passing sentence, must consider the role of an accused in question carefully and in detail. What we say is this: That there are three accused, particularly, all of whom have been convicted after trials at this institution whose sentences you should play close regard to. The first is Krstic's. He was convicted, inter alia, of genocide and ultimately received 35 years in prison. Blagojevic was convicted, inter alia, of aiding and abetting genocide, 15 years imprisonment. And Jokic was convicted, inter alia, of extermination, nine years imprisonment. These offences are, whichever way one looks at it, far more serious than the offences for which Milan Gvero is charged and stands to be convicted, even in the worst eventuality on this particular indictment. Bearing this in mind, for the Prosecution to suggest that Milan Gvero, even taking the Prosecution case at its highest, that he should receive a sentence of life imprisonment with a 30-year minimum term, is nothing short of absurd. The reality is, and I make no apology for saying this, that the Prosecution submissions as to sentence are of no help to you whatsoever when you come to determine sentence in this case. Now, Your Honour, there are a few matters in mitigation which I wish to point to. Interestingly, the evidence in mitigation that I rely upon has basically emerged organically during this trial, inadvertently, really, when the Court has been dealing with other topics or witnesses have, and I'm going to run through this very quickly simply by pointing some page numbers. The first point is we'd invite you to look at page 75, paragraph 135, and page 116, paragraph 53, of our final brief, in relation to Asim Hodzic. Secondly, we'd ask you to look at page 115 to 117, paragraphs 50 to 54, which is material basically addressing the indictment, but it contains some material that you may find useful in relation to mitigation. Third, we'd invite you to look at General Simic's reference to the Batkovic camp which were, you may think, entirely unprompted on the 21st of November of last year at 28601. Fourth, page 91, paragraph 11 of our brief, in relation to the document P28 issued by General Gvero in relation to the correctness of this document, there's either reliance placed on it by the Prosecution in their closing argument at 34138 on the 3rd of September. And, finally, General Gvero's distribution of various ICRC documents in Serbian to his troops, described in the evidence of Skrbic at 156 -- I'll give that again, 15569 to 15572. Next, voluntary surrender. It's not clear in the Prosecution brief, at paragraph 2831, if they actually concede that that is what General Gvero did, but Your Honours know, from the various provisional release applications in this case and also the decisions that you have made, that it's not been in dispute. It can be said that General Gvero voluntarily surrendered, and I urge that as a piece of mitigation on his behalf. Next, his health. Now, Milan Gvero is not only the oldest man on trial in this case, he is now the oldest person in detention at the UNDU. As you know, he suffers from relatively poor health. You know about all this from the various reports that you have seen in our various provisional release applications. In particular, you know that he will shortly require open-heart surgery. The fact that health is an issue that a Chamber can take into account, in terms of sentencing, was dealt with in the Strugar appeals judgement of the 17th of July, 2008, where that Court said: "After examining the relevant evidence, the Appeal Chamber considers that Strugar's deteriorating health since the trial judgement was rendered must be considered as a mitigating factor." Your Honours, in conclusion and without wanting to labour an obvious, sombre, but above all else important point, we can only urge you, on behalf of Milan Gvero, that in the event you convict him on any count in this indictment, that you pass a sentence that does not inevitably mean that he will die in prison. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Are there any questions? Not at the moment, anyway, but we might have Monday. I don't know. So we stand -- yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify the record, we agree that Milan Gvero and General Miletic self-surrendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Obviously, we're grateful from this side of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you. So we'll reconvene Monday morning at 9.00. On Monday, Mr. Haynes, I assume, would finish within the two and a half hours allotted or allocated. Do you intend to ask for time for rebuttal or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, my intention right now is to ask for 15 to 20 minutes of rebuttal, specifically to answer some of the factual allegations made by the Borovcanin Defence. For any of the other cases, I don't see anything right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. We stand adjourned to Monday, 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of September, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
